pages.title: KDataForge
pages.description: Create and patch Satisfactory content with YAML packs, without writing C++.

sections.heading: KDataForge
sections.text: KDataForge is a YAML-driven runtime content framework for Satisfactory. Put pack files under <your-mod>/DataForge/**/*.yml to rebalance existing content, generate new classes and assets, or ship integrations with other mods. Generated content has save-stable identity, and the in-game editor can inspect live objects and export drafts. Packs can expose typed settings that players change without touching YAML, and read them back through typed references and templates. In multiplayer, every process loads its own pack set. KDataForge does not negotiate checksums or stream applied operations; only pack configuration values are sent from the host to clients.

sections.heading: For Pack Authors
sections.text: If you want to rebalance a recipe, add an item, or ship a small content pack without touching C++, start with Getting Started . It builds the smallest possible pack and verifies that it loaded. Use KDataForge Tools to edit YAML, review diagnostics, and run a full pack check before starting the game. For existing KPatchwork pull-request policy checks, see Lint Your Pack . Continue with the Task Guides , including Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock for the most common first content chain. Once you know the pack shape, use Features to understand a capability and Reference for exact schema or API details. Property Types and Operations explain the codec every patch value uses. Recipes and Items cover two common document types. To let players tune your pack, see Pack Configuration , Templates and Typed References and the walkthrough Player-Configurable Balancing . The Examples section contains complete multi-capability packs such as Balancing and End-to-End Pack . Use these when you want to see several document types wired together.

sections.heading: For Mod Developers / Contributors
sections.text: If you are extending KDataForge, adding a native document handler, embedding it from another mod, or reviewing the pipeline, use Internals & Architecture . It is contributor material, not a prerequisite for authoring a pack. Architecture walks the full data flow from filesystem scan to reflection-based property edits, and Module Structure maps the plugin’s runtime modules. The Reference section contains the normative detail. YAML Schema is the complete grammar, Handler Template is a reference C++ implementation for a new handler, API Design covers the public API surface for third-party mods, and Editor Integration documents KDF.ApplyToAssets for applying YAML packs directly onto assets inside the Unreal Editor. The Blueprint Config API is the surface for building a pack settings screen, and Config Expressions is the grammar of config: conditions.

sections.heading: Commands
sections.text: KDataForge exposes a small set of chat commands (typed in-game as /kdf ... ) and console variables for inspecting and controlling a running instance without editing files: Command Where Effect /kdf report chat Prints the load report: packs, applied documents, ops, warnings, errors /kdf reload chat (host/server admin) Restores KDF property baselines, rescans all pack files (including edited configuration values files: hot values apply, cold values report “restart required”), and re-applies the normal stage pipeline. See Smart reload KDF.Reload console (host/server) Same smart reload as /kdf reload ; useful for dedicated-server consoles and launch automation /kdf editor chat (host) Toggles the in-game editor: browse content, edit properties live, undo/redo, and export changes to YAML KDF.Editor console Same as /kdf editor /kdf debug on|off chat Flips global debug logging (same switch as KDF.Debug ). Bare /kdf debug toggles the current state KDF.Debug 1 console (or launch arg -KDFDebug ) Global debug logging : one [KDF DEBUG] line per applied op, including editor edits. Narrower scopes: debug: true per document or in pack.yml KDF.ApplyToAssets [PathFilter] console ( UE editor builds only ) Applies loaded YAML directly onto editor assets and marks packages dirty. See Editor Integration /kdf config dump [pack] chat Lists the pack configuration fields with value, default and effective value. See Pack Configuration /kdf config set <pack>:<id> <value> chat (host/server admin) Sets a pending configuration value (lists take comma separated elements) /kdf config apply [pack] chat (host/server admin) Saves pending values and reloads when a hot field changed; reports keys that need a restart KDF.Config.Dump , KDF.Config.Set , KDF.Config.Apply console Console versions of the three commands above KDF.Template "<text>" [pack] console Expands {prefix:body} templates, see Templates KDF.Config.Expr "<expr>" [pack] console Evaluates a config: expression, see Config Expressions /kdf-reflection [options] chat (host/server) Exports reflected classes, structs, enums, defaults, functions, game settings, Blueprint mappings, and assets. Without options it uses the full profile. See Reflection Export KDF.DumpReflection [options] console (host/server) The same export with time-sliced game-thread work. Without options it writes no functions, non-texture asset indexes or flattened classes; pass --assets --functions --flattened for the full profile KDF.ValidateReflection [--out] console Runs acceptance checks against completed reflection output

sections.heading: Quick Start
sections.text: Create <your-mod>/DataForge/pack.yml : ref : MyTweaks name : My Tweaks version : 1.0.0 Then create <your-mod>/DataForge/my-tweaks.cdo.yml : type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.5 Start the game. The recipe now smelts twice as fast. Use /kdf report in chat to inspect the load report. After changing YAML, use /kdf reload for a smart live re-apply; restart when changing frozen content registrations or other restart-bound state . Prefer a UI? /kdf editor opens the in-game editor with live property editing and YAML export. For local pack validation, use KDataForge Tools to catch static schema errors before shipping.

pages.title: Internals & Architecture
pages.description: Runtime pipeline, C++ module organization, persistence, and contributor-facing design contracts.

sections.heading: Internals & Architecture
sections.text: This section is background reading, not a prerequisite. You can write a YAML pack, load it, and balance a recipe without knowing any of it. It’s here for the curious. It’s also here for anyone extending KDataForge itself with a new handler, who wants to understand the data flow, the subsystems, and the module boundaries before touching code. Architecture walks through the full pipeline. It covers the filesystem scan, the pack configuration flow (configuration is read first), YAML parsing, the fixed stage order, the reflection engine that turns a property path into a live edit, savegame persistence for generated content, configuration value synchronization, and the current multiplayer boundaries. Module Structure covers how the plugin’s four runtime modules ( KDataForgeApi , KDataForgeYaml , KDataForge , KDataForgeEditorUI ) are laid out on disk. It explains why they’re split that way, and the dependency rules that keep the public API tiny and the dedicated-server build lean.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.description: System design, data flow, subsystems, savegame persistence strategy, and current multiplayer boundaries.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: KDataForge is a data-driven runtime content editing framework . Users, and other mods, describe changes to game content in YAML documents. The framework parses these documents once at startup, validates them, and applies them through Unreal’s reflection system in a fixed, deterministic stage order. Authors use <your-mod>/DataForge/**/*.yml . The scanner itself starts at the Unreal project root, which is FactoryGame/ in a packaged game. It recognizes directories named DataForge , the legacy name data-editor , and any directory containing pack.yml . Roots may nest, and each YAML file is assigned only to its deepest enclosing root. An implicit pack ref and name come from the detected root’s parent directory, so an explicit stable ref is recommended. Pack configuration is the first thing a load reads: after the scan, the *.config.yml definitions and values files of every pack are loaded into UKDFConfigRegistry , before pack conditions are evaluated and before any document is parsed. The template pre-pass then replaces cfg: / session: / ags: / option: values and evaluates entry-level conditions, so the stages only ever see plain documents. See Pack Configuration Flow .

sections.heading: Lifecycle Integration (SML)
sections.text: KDataForge hooks SML’s module lifecycle via two auto-discovered root modules, UKDFGameInstanceModule and UKDFWorldModule . UKDFGameInstanceModule acts across three phases. During CONSTRUCTION, its built-in handlers exist (the subsystem’s Initialize ), and this is the window in which third-party mods register their own handlers. During INITIALIZATION, UKDFSubsystem::RunInitialLoad() performs the full scan, parse, and apply pass. This runs before any world or save loads, so CDO edits and generated classes exist before anything references them. The full pass runs only once per GameInstance. During POST_INITIALIZATION, the load report is logged. UKDFWorldModule runs per world. It registers the /kdf chat command and the configuration sync subsystem. During world INITIALIZATION, after save deserialization and before actor BeginPlay , it first tells UKDFSubsystem that the world is ready (which reloads once if a document was deferred for want of session settings), then drains queued content registration, applies schematic/research registry removals, then asks UKDFContentRemoveSubsystem to sweep save-restored recipes. Registration runs first, so an explicit removal wins when both name the same class. SML guarantees all modules receive CONSTRUCTION before any receives INITIALIZATION, which makes the third-party handler registration window safe.

sections.heading: Core Components
sections.text: Component Type Responsibility UKDFSubsystem GameInstanceSubsystem Owns loader, handler registry, class/object caches, patch records, registrations, removals, and world rules FKDFPackScanner static Filesystem discovery (pruned recursive walk, pack.yml manifests) FKDFYamlParser static (KDataForgeYaml) ryml façade, the only YAML entry point; thread-safe parse, deterministic hand-written emitter FKDFConditionEvaluator static Document, pack and entry conditions: evaluation, including config: expressions UKDFConfigRegistry member of subsystem Owns every UKDFConfigDescription (key <pack>:<id> ), the values files, and the value lifecycle UKDFConfigDescription UObject family One configured field; subclasses per widget kind. Public Blueprint surface ( UKDFConfigBlueprintLibrary ) FKDFTemplateEngine static {prefix:body} templates, typed references, and the config: expression parser IKDFTemplateProvider interface (KDataForgeApi) Extension point that resolves one template prefix; built-ins cover cfg , session , ags , option and reflection targets FKDFColdPropertyCatalog member of subsystem Classifies properties as hot, cold or newActors for restart advice FKDFReloadScheduler member of subsystem Debounces automatic reloads caused by setting or host value changes AKDFConfigSyncSubsystem AModSubsystem Replicates the host’s effective configuration values to clients FKDFPropertyResolver static Property path → (FProperty, value ptr) resolution incl. containers and object dereference FKDFValueCodec static Bidirectional YAML ↔ FProperty conversion FKDFOpEngine static The 22 property operations with per-kind capability matrix FKDFVanillaCache member of subsystem First-write snapshots for editor diff, undo, and changes-only export FKDFDynamicContentRegistry member of subsystem Creates deterministic generated classes/assets and reconstructs missing generated classes as tombstones UKDFCdoHandler handler ( cdo ) CDOs, data-asset instances, allAssetsOfClass , tag matcher, actor patches UKDFSublevelHandler handler ( sublevel ) Blocks RefinedRDLib/KBFL sublevel descriptor assets during CDOChanges UKDFContentClassHandler handler base Generates item/resource/building/unlock/recipe/schematic/research classes; queues registration/removal UKDFAssetHandler handler ( asset ) Decodes pack-relative 2D images into transient texture assets UKDFDataAssetHandler handler ( dataasset ) Creates UDataAsset instances, applies instanced lists, and requests optional consumer rescans UKDFCurveHandler handler ( curve ) Creates or edits UCurveFloat and UCurveVector assets during the Assets stage UKDFGameTagHandler handler ( gametag ) Runtime gameplay tag registration UKDFLocalizationHandler handler ( localization ) Runtime namespace/culture text registration UKDFSinkPointsHandler handler ( sinkpoints ) Queues per-world AWESOME Sink table values UKDFResourceNodeHandler handler ( resourcenode ) Registers descriptor/node-type purge rules for live worlds UKDFActorPatchSubsystem WorldSubsystem Applies actor patches at world begin play + every spawn UKDFContentRemoveSubsystem WorldSubsystem Orchestrates recipe sweeps and exposes per-world removal queries/counts UKDFResourceNodeSubsystem WorldSubsystem Purges matching nodes, local mesh actors, scanner data, and radar/scanner caches FKDFRecipeRemoval static/native hooks Blocks future recipe adds and removes recipes restored from server save data AKDFChatCommand chat command /kdf report , /kdf editor , /kdf debug on|off

sections.heading: The Reflection Engine
sections.text: Resolution ( FKDFPropertyPath → FKDFPropertyResolver ) turns a parsed path such as mIngredients[0].Amount into a value, segment by segment, supporting name lookup (including Blueprint authored names), array/set index access, and map key lookup. Dereferencing through object-typed members is also supported, which is what makes mSomeComponent.Property and default subobjects reachable. Conversion ( FKDFValueCodec ) supports bool, all numerics, enums (typed and byte-based), FString/FName/FText (with localized key , ns , and source fields), object/class references (hard and soft), structs (native text form, map form, positional sequence form), arrays, sets, and maps, with everything else falling back to a generic text-based conversion path. This fallback is what makes “every reflectable type” honest, without needing hundreds of hand-written cases. Operations ( FKDFOpEngine ) validate each op against the leaf property kind before applying it: multiply on an FString produces a diagnostic, not a silent no-op. FGameplayTagContainer is special-cased so tag containers accept append/prepend/remove/clear/set with plain tag names. The full list of the 22 supported operations, their signatures, and which property kinds accept each one is covered in Operations . The property kinds themselves, and how a mIngredients[0].Amount -style path resolves, are covered in Property Types .

sections.heading: Vanilla Snapshots
sections.text: Before the first write to any (object, property path) pair, the original value is exported to canonical text and stored in FKDFVanillaCache . The in-game editor uses this snapshot for its Diff tab, undo workflow, and changes-only export.

sections.heading: Runtime Actor Patches
sections.text: applyToSpawnedActors: true on a cdo patch registers an FKDFActorPatch . UKDFActorPatchSubsystem applies the ops to all matching pre-existing actors at world begin play, and to every matching actor the moment it spawns. This guarantees YAML values win even where per-instance state, such as save-restored values or archetypes, would override plain CDO defaults. Exact-class or subclass matching is controlled by applyToSubclasses . Actor-instance operations are direct writes. They do not compare against vanilla snapshots and do not preserve player-modified or save-restored values. The same class-scoped operation list is applied to every matching instance. The cdo document type, its properties: / applyToSpawnedActors / applyToSubclasses fields, and the CDO/data-asset/tag-matcher targeting model are covered in full in Patching (type: cdo) and Targeting .

sections.heading: Per-world Registration and Removal
sections.text: GameInstance handlers cannot mutate world managers because no gameplay world exists during the initial YAML pass. They retain deterministic requests instead: recipe, schematic, and research entries queue SML content registration; document-level remove: on those same types queues exact-class removal rules; sinkpoints queues Sink table writes; resourcenode queues descriptor/node-type purge rules; cdo with applyToSpawnedActors queues actor-class patch rules. UKDFWorldModule drains registrations before removals during world INITIALIZATION. SML directly removes schematic and research classes. Recipes need FKDFRecipeRemoval : process-wide hooks block future singular and batch adds, while the per-world sweep removes recipes already restored from the server save before AFGRecipeManager::BeginPlay builds derived caches. Resource Node purges use a separate four-point schedule because level actors, streamed levels, spawns, and late descriptor retargeting become visible at different times.

sections.heading: Pack Configuration Flow
sections.text: Both entry points, RunInitialLoad and ReloadAll , run the same pipeline: Scan. The pack scanner finds packs, manifests and files. Configuration first. Every pack’s *.config.yml definitions and its values file are loaded. Descriptions keep their identity across reloads; definitions that vanished are marked stale. The effective value of each field is decided here: a hot field follows the stored value (or the multiplayer host’s), a cold field keeps the value the running content was built with once the first load has finished. Pack conditions and dependencies. pack.yml conditions run with access to config: values. A pack that is switched off keeps its descriptions, marked not active. Parse the documents of the remaining packs. Pre-pass. Typed references and pre-pass templates are substituted in every document, and entry-level conditions: are evaluated and stripped. A document that needs session: or ags: values before a world exists is deferred. The pass also records which hot fields feed cold contexts so that the result can say restart advised . Stages run in the fixed order. Apply-time templates are expanded per operation, when the operand is about to be written. Finish. Category classes are resolved (generated classes exist only after the Items stage) and queued description events are broadcast. Events never fire in the middle of a load. Applying changes from a UI saves pending values to the values file and, when a hot field changed, runs exactly one reload. Automatic reloads (a changed session setting, a changed host value) go through a debounce, and a burst guard suppresses runaway reload loops; user-initiated applies are never delayed. When the world is ready, the world module tells the subsystem. If a document was deferred, or a session: / ags: / option: value that a document used has changed, KDataForge reloads once with the world’s values. Values files are plain YAML written atomically. Only the player’s own stored values are ever written; host values and pending values stay in memory.

sections.heading: Savegame Persistence Strategy
sections.text: Dynamically created content must survive save/load with valid class paths. Class generation relies on SML’s FClassGenerator::GenerateSimpleClass (root-set, parent layout copy, CDO auto-created). Class identity is id-based and deterministic : package /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef> , class Gen_<PackRef>_<Id> . It is never derived from file paths or load order, so renaming a file must not orphan save data. Classes survive save and load because they are created during GameInstance INITIALIZATION, strictly before any save loads. The save serialiser resolves class paths through StaticFindObject before attempting a linker load, so resolution hits the in-memory class. No cooked package is needed. The constraint is that generated classes keep the parent’s layout: no new reflected properties and no new components. All variation lives in CDO defaults. This covers descriptors, recipes, schematics, and unlocks fully, but it does not cover new buildables with custom components. A global generated-content manifest at Saved/KDataForge/GeneratedClasses.json records every generated class ever created , including its pack, id, and parent path. At startup, recorded classes missing from the current YAML are recreated as tombstones : functional but hidden and deprecated, so old saves load cleanly even after packs are removed. Because the manifest is global, class-path resolution works for any save, not just ones whose header was written by KDataForge. Renames use redirects: in pack.yml ( OldId: NewId ), which feeds FCoreRedirects so old save class paths resolve to the renamed class. Per-save state is held by AKDFStateSubsystem : AModSubsystem with SaveGame properties that store the applied-pack history: pack ref, version, and timestamp per entry. Removal features have separate persistence rules: schematic and research-tree registry removals write nothing to the save and reverse next session after the pack is removed, but do not revoke purchases or research progress; recipe removal mutates the saved available-recipe list, then self-heals on a later load without the pack when purchased schematics reapply unlocks; resourcenode destroys world actors, and vanilla can persist those destruction tombstones even after the pack is removed. It is a potentially irreversible world migration. See Recipes , Schematics , Research Trees , and Resources before using those paths. See Recipes , Schematics , and Unlocks for the document types that drive this generated-class path, and Renaming Content Safely for how redirects: is used in practice.

sections.heading: Multiplayer Boundaries
sections.text: Every game process performs its own initial YAML load. The current source has no pack-checksum handshake, mismatch rejection, or server-to-client operation stream. Install the same packs and versions on the server and every client. UKDFRemoteCallObject::Server_ApplySetOp is a host-gated RPC scaffold. The editor UI does not call it, and there is no general Server_ApplyOps pipeline. Treat live editor changes as local process state, not synchronized multiplayer state. The one thing that is synchronized is pack configuration values, and nothing else: The server (host or dedicated server) is the authority. AKDFConfigSyncSubsystem replicates its effective values, each flagged hot or cold, to every client. A client keeps them in memory as host overrides. Its own values file is never written from them, and leaving the session restores its local values. A differing hot value makes the client reload (debounced) so its content matches the host. A differing cold value only raises a host-mismatch state and event, once per key and join. Changes come from the host, or from a dedicated-server administrator through Server_ApplyConfigChanges , which is permission-checked on the server and answered with Client_ConfigApplyResult . A listen-server client cannot change values. This is value synchronization, not a pack handshake: nothing verifies that clients have the same packs. Install the same packs and versions everywhere.

sections.heading: Determinism Rules (load-bearing)
sections.text: Stages execute in fixed EKDFStage enum order. Pack dependencies are hard topological constraints. Packs with missing, self-referential, or transitively invalid dependencies are rejected. Dependency cycles are rejected. Among packs whose dependencies are ready, higher priority runs first and ref ascending breaks ties. Within a stage, handlers are ordered by priority descending then root type ascending. Documents follow their dependency-ordered packs, then same-stage include: constraints and relative path. Map iteration never determines apply order. FKDFNode maps preserve document order. Every process must see the same pack set and inputs to produce the same result. KDataForge does not verify this across multiplayer peers yet. For the module layout that hosts these subsystems and handlers, see Module Structure . For the YAML fields that condition evaluation, targeting, and the stage/handler pipeline actually parse, see the YAML Schema reference.

pages.title: Module Structure
pages.description: C++ module organization, folder layout, and dependency rules across KDataForge's five runtime modules.

sections.heading: Module Structure
sections.text: If you only ever write YAML packs, none of this applies to you. Packs load through KDataForge.uasset and never see a module boundary. This page is for two other audiences: people contributing to KDataForge’s own C++ (the runtime and the handlers it ships with), and third-party mod authors who want to register a native handler for a document root type KDataForge doesn’t cover built-in. Both audiences need to know which module their code belongs in and which dependencies they’re allowed to take on. The split isn’t arbitrary. It marks the difference between a stable public contract and internals that can change release to release. KDataForge ships as one Unreal plugin split into five separate C++ modules rather than one. Fewer DLL boundaries generally mean fewer allocator and export headaches, so this split is deliberate, not incidental. Each boundary exists to isolate something specific: a public API surface, an exception-throwing dependency, or the in-game editor’s UI dependencies.

sections.heading: Why the split exists
sections.text: Three concerns drive where a module boundary sits: Contract isolation. Third-party mods that want to add a handler must link against something stable. Bundling that contract into the same module as the fast-moving loader/reflection internals would mean every internal refactor risks an ABI break for downstream mods. KDataForgeApi exists so that contract can stay frozen while everything else evolves underneath it. See API Design for what that contract actually contains. Exception containment. The vendored YAML parser (rapidyaml) reports errors by throwing, but the rest of the codebase doesn’t build with C++ exceptions enabled. Rather than flip on exceptions plugin-wide, only the module that wraps the parser does. UI dependency isolation. The in-game editor pulls in InputCore , UMG , Slate , SlateCore , and AppFramework . Keeping it in KDataForgeEditorUI stops those dependencies from leaking into the loader/reflection runtime, even though the module itself is still declared as a Runtime module.

sections.heading: The five modules
sections.text: All five modules are declared "Type": "Runtime" in the .uplugin manifest, including KDataForgeEditorUI . KDataForgeApi contains the public handler contract. Third-party handlers derive against it, while registration also links the main KDataForge module. KDataForgeYaml is the YAML backend, wrapping rapidyaml behind a façade, and it’s the only module with exceptions enabled. KDataForge is the main runtime, holding the loader, the reflection engine, the subsystems, the built-in handlers, the chat command, and networking. KDataForgeReflection owns standalone reflection export and metadata tooling without adding those concerns to main runtime. KDataForgeEditorUI is the in-game editor UI, built with Slate, and its Build.cs currently declares the UI dependency set unconditionally. That’s a deliberate naming trap worth calling out. “EditorUI” refers to an in-game editor window rendered with hand-built Slate while the game is running, not to Unreal Editor-only code. Nothing in that module is gated behind WITH_EDITOR , and none of its dependencies are editor-only modules. It has to build and link cleanly anywhere the plugin loads it.

sections.heading: KDataForgeApi the public contract
sections.text: Third-party mods use this module for handler types and keep it intentionally tiny: Source/KDataForgeApi/Public/ ├── KDFDataEditorHandler.h ├── KDFHandlerBase.h ├── KDFNode.h └── KDFTypes.h Its dependency list is just Core , CoreUObject , and Engine , nothing else. That’s not an accident of an early prototype. It’s rule #2 below: adding a dependency here is treated as an API-breaking decision, because every third-party handler mod inherits whatever this module pulls in. The types you’ll actually work with here ( FKDFNode , UKDFHandlerBase , IKDFDataEditorHandler ) are covered in API Design . A worked handler implementation against this exact module lives on the Handler Template page.

sections.heading: KDataForgeYaml the YAML backend
sections.text: This module exists for one reason: to keep exceptions from leaking anywhere else in the plugin. KDFYamlParser.h parses a document that throws ryml::Callbacks::error and turns it into a clean FKDFNode tree or an error string, entirely inside this module: Source/KDataForgeYaml/ ├── Public/ KDFYamlParser.h (façade the only entry point) ├── Private/ KDFYamlParser.cpp (ryml + a deterministic hand-written emitter) └── ThirdParty/ryml/rapidyaml.hpp (v0.15.2 amalgamation vendored, never edited) bEnableExceptions = true is set only in this module’s .Build.cs . The reasoning is spelled out right next to it: rapidyaml reports parse errors through a callback that throws, and that has to stay contained to this wrapper. The public surface only ever returns FKDFNode trees and error strings, never a ryml type or an exception across a module boundary. Its own dependencies are Core , CoreUObject , and KDataForgeApi (for FKDFNode ). Nothing pulls FactoryGame or SML in here.

sections.heading: KDataForge the main runtime
sections.text: This is where nearly everything lives: the loader, the reflection engine, the built-in handlers, the subsystems, and the pieces that don’t get their own module because they’re not a public contract, an exception boundary, or an editor-only concern. Layering inside it happens at the folder level, not via further module splits: Source/KDataForge/{Public,Private}/ ├── Reflection/ KDFPropertyPath · KDFValueCodec · KDFOpEngine · KDFVanillaCache · KDFPatchUtil ├── Loader/ KDFPackScanner · KDFConditionEvaluator · KDFLoaderTypes · KDFPackInfo ├── Config/ KDFConfigRegistry · KDFConfigDescription (+ per-kind subclasses) · │ KDFConfigBlueprintLibrary · KDFReloadScheduler (pack configuration) ├── Template/ KDFTemplateEngine · KDFTemplatePrePass · KDFConfigExpression · │ KDFColdProperties · KDFWorldBoundTracker ├── Content/ KDFDynamicContent (class/asset generation, manifest, tombstones) · │ KDFRecipeRemoval ├── Subsystems/ KDFSubsystem · KDFActorPatchSubsystem · KDFStateSubsystem · │ KDFContentRemoveSubsystem · KDFResourceNodeSubsystem ├── Handlers/ KDFCdoHandler · KDFAssetHandler · KDFCurveHandler · KDFGameTagHandler · │ KDFContentClassHandler family (Class/Item/Resource/Building/Recipe/ │ Schematic/Research/Unlock) · KDFDataAssetHandler · │ KDFSinkPointsHandler · KDFLocalizationHandler · KDFSublevelHandler · │ KDFResourceNodeHandler ├── Commands/ KDFChatCommand ├── Module/ KDFGameInstanceModule · KDFWorldModule (SML root modules) ├── Net/ KDFRemoteCallObject (host-gated RPC scaffold + admin config RPC) · │ KDFConfigSyncSubsystem (host config values → clients) └── EditorIntegration/ KDFEditorApply (WITH_EDITOR-gated, private-only: `KDF.ApplyToAssets` console command bakes cdo documents directly onto UE-editor assets) EditorIntegration/ is the one genuinely editor-only corner of the whole plugin, and it earns that by being gated behind WITH_EDITOR at the file level rather than by living in its own module. It never ships to Shipping or dedicated-server builds, and it has no public header at all, since nothing outside this one .cpp needs to call into it. Net/ contains a host-gated Server_ApplySetOp RPC scaffold. The current editor does not call it, and there is no checksum handshake or operation stream. See the current multiplayer boundaries in Architecture . Main runtime dependency list is broad: Core , CoreUObject , Engine , Projects , Json , GameplayTags , NetCore , AssetRegistry , ImageWrapper , RenderCore , RHI , the DummyHeaders stub module, FactoryGame , and SML , plus KDataForgeApi and KDataForgeYaml . The ImageWrapper , RenderCore , and RHI trio backs type: asset documents, turning arbitrary 2D image files into runtime UTexture2D assets through KDFAssetHandler .

sections.heading: KDataForgeReflection exporter
sections.text: Reflection export stays in separate runtime module. Main KDataForge module does not depend on it. Module provides KDF.DumpReflection , /kdf-reflection , validation command, metadata commandlet, Blueprint loading, native/Blueprint maps, asset indexes, uncapped texture image export, and background JSON/ZIP writing. Its direct dependencies are Core , CoreUObject , Engine , Projects , Json , AssetRegistry , ImageCore , DummyHeaders , FactoryGame , and SML . See Reflection Export for commands and output contract. UKDFReflectionWorldModule is non-root and is spawned by UKDFWorldModule through soft class path; SML allows only one root world module per plugin and world-module type.

sections.heading: KDataForgeEditorUI the in-game editor
sections.text: Kept as its own module so Slate, UMG, and AppFramework stay isolated from the main runtime module: Source/KDataForgeEditorUI/ ├── Public/ KDFEditorSubsystem.h · KDFEditorModel.h └── Private/ SKDFEditorWindow.* · KDFEditorStyle.h (pure code-built Slate, no UMG assets) The editor window needs to read the loader’s pack manifests, walk FKDFNode trees, and apply ops through the same reflection engine the runtime uses to build its Diff and Apply tabs. Because of that, it depends on all three other modules: KDataForgeApi , KDataForgeYaml , and KDataForge , alongside InputCore , UMG , Slate , SlateCore , AppFramework (for SColorPicker ), AssetRegistry , FactoryGame , and SML . The wiring between this window and the runtime it edits is covered on Editor Integration .

sections.heading: Dependency graph
sections.text: Arrows below point from a module to what it depends on. KDataForgeApi sits at the bottom with the smallest footprint by design. Reflection exporter is independent from main runtime and YAML/API layers: KDataForgeEditorUI → KDataForge, KDataForgeYaml, KDataForgeApi (+ InputCore, UMG, Slate, SlateCore, AppFramework, AssetRegistry, FactoryGame, SML) KDataForgeReflection → Core, CoreUObject, Engine, Projects, Json, AssetRegistry, DummyHeaders, FactoryGame, SML ▲ KDataForge → KDataForgeYaml, KDataForgeApi (+ Engine, Projects, Json, GameplayTags, NetCore, AssetRegistry, ImageWrapper, RenderCore, RHI, DummyHeaders, FactoryGame, SML) ▲ KDataForgeYaml → KDataForgeApi [bEnableExceptions] (+ Core, CoreUObject) ▲ KDataForgeApi (Core, CoreUObject, Engine only) Link-dependency lesson (Shipping builds): the dev-editor target resolves symbols that the modular Shipping DLLs do not. EKeys needs InputCore , UModContentRegistry needs SML , and FKDFYamlParser needs KDataForgeYaml . A Shipping package run is the real link check, not a dev-editor compile.

sections.heading: Rules for contributors
sections.text: These aren’t style preferences. Each one closes off a class of bug that’s already bitten this plugin once: ryml types never cross the KDataForgeYaml boundary. The façade returns FKDFNode trees and error strings only. Exceptions exist only inside that module, per bEnableExceptions above. KDataForgeApi stays tiny and dependency-free ( Core , CoreUObject , Engine ). Adding a dependency there is an API-breaking decision for every third-party handler mod. Treat it as such. No editor-only module dependencies anywhere. The plugin must build for Shipping and dedicated servers. Editor-only code, if ever needed, goes behind Target.bBuildEditor in .Build.cs plus WITH_EDITOR guards (see EditorIntegration/ above for the one place this already applies). Handlers live in the main module or in third-party mods. Third-party handler types derive against KDataForgeApi ; calling UKDFSubsystem::RegisterHandler also requires KDataForge . Handlers never include loader or scanner internals. Everything they need arrives via the context structs that the Handler Template walks through. All five modules share the same build settings: CppStandard = Cpp20 , PCHUsage = UseExplicitOrSharedPCHs , bLegacyPublicIncludePaths = false , and the project’s clang-format is enforced across all of them. For how these modules cooperate at runtime, the fixed stage pipeline, the reflection engine, and savegame persistence, see Architecture .

pages.title: Examples
pages.description: Complete worked galleries that combine multiple property types, operations, and document types into one realistic pack.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.text: This section is home to worked examples : real, copy-pasteable YAML that combines several concepts at once, the way an actual pack looks in practice. It’s deliberately different from the other two teaching sections in this documentation. Features explains one capability or document type at a time. Task Guides walk a single goal from start to finish and explain each step as they go. The pages here skip that step-by-step framing. Instead they read like a gallery you can search or a reference chain you can walk. Use them once you already know roughly what you’re doing and want to see it done for real, with several types wired together. If this is your first time here, Getting Started and the Property Types / Operations / Targeting / Conditions & Packs pages in Features are the better starting point. Come back here once those are familiar and you want end-to-end examples instead of isolated snippets. Every individual document type ( item , recipe , schematic , cdo , and the rest) also has its own dedicated page under Features. The full YAML grammar lives in Reference .

sections.heading: Example packs
sections.text: ADA Voice-over from a WAV File imports PCM16 audio as a Wwise event, connects it to FGMessage.mAudioEvent , and configures a milestone trigger. Player-Configurable Balancing is a complete pack with five typed settings, category classes, cfg: references, a template description and a config: condition. It is the sample pack’s configuration part, built step by step. Two pages below are patch-only collections with many small type: cdo examples. Two are build-a-whole-thing packs that chain several document types into finished content. The fifth is a focused complete pack for a Repeat-Purchase Schematic (KLIB) with generated curves. The sixth is a per-type creation gallery of type: dataasset examples, one for each KAPI data asset type, the same spirit as Balancing but for generating new instances instead of patching existing ones. The seventh is a single build-a-whole-thing tree for one KAPI type, UKAPIDeliveryTask . Balancing covers rebalancing base-game content that already exists: recipes, items, resources, equipment, consumables, radioactivity, belt speed, schematics, milestones, research trees, vehicles, trains, creatures, categories, and bulk tag-matched edits across many targets at once. All of it works through type: cdo patches against existing classes, and nothing is generated. Power & Machines covers the buildable-tuning half of patching: power consumption, manufacturing speed, generator output, extractor cycle time, pipeline flow limits, power storage capacity, drone station logistics, and runtime actor patches that also affect already-placed buildings. A Complete Building walks the full reference chain for a dynamically generated building, in dependency order: buildable class → building descriptor → build recipe → production recipes → schematic → sink points. These are six files, and each one references the class path the previous file produced. End-to-End Pack builds one realistic pack from an item, a recipe, a schematic with an inline unlock, sink points, a German localization file, a dynamic KAPI data asset, and a cdo edit to another mod’s data-asset instances. It also shows how to rename a generated id safely with redirects: once the pack has shipped. Repeat-Purchase Schematic (KLIB) is a complete UKLUnlockMaxRepeatPurchases pack with generated cost and reward curves, level-specific overrides, a result table, and the runtime semantics behind each purchase. Adding KAPI Data Assets covers type: dataasset creation for every KAPI PrimaryDataAsset type: air collector, cleaner, modular miner, slug breeding, and extractor/resource allow-lists. Delivery Task Trees builds one complete UKAPIDeliveryTask tree from scratch: five nodes (including negative coordinates), a multi-flag mParentTask , repeated-parent thresholds, the full Endless field set, and a schematic force-unlock example. For a normative catalog of every base-game FGUnlock subclass, including its settable properties and caveats, use Base-Game Unlock Classes . All seven assume a pack living at <your-mod>/DataForge/ , the canonical author root used throughout these docs.

pages.title: ADA Voice-over from a WAV File
pages.description: Complete pack example that imports a PCM16 WAV, creates an ADA message, and ties it to purchasing Hub Upgrade 1.

sections.heading: ADA Voice-over from a WAV File
sections.text: This pack imports your recording through Wwise and assigns it to a new ADA message. The message becomes eligible when Hub Upgrade 1 is purchased. Triggers observe new events: use a fresh save or choose a milestone that has not been purchased yet. Previewing sound alone does not mark the ADA message as played.

sections.heading: Pack files
sections.text: DataForge/ADAExample/ pack.yml welcome.sound.yml welcome-message.dataasset.yml audio/ welcome.wav Record or export welcome.wav as PCM16 WAV , mono or stereo, 48000 Hz. Suggested spoken text: “Welcome, pioneer. Your first Hub upgrade is complete.” This is your audio file; the YAML does not synthesize speech. Keep the file below 64 MiB. pack.yml ref : ADAExample name : ADA Voice-over Example version : 1.0.0 welcome.sound.yml type : sound sounds : - id : AdaWelcome file : audio/welcome.wav name : ADA welcome volume description : Controls playback volume for the welcome message. category : Voices subCategory : ADA welcome-message.dataasset.yml type : dataasset assets : - id : WelcomeMessage class : /Script/FactoryGame.FGMessage properties : - path : mTitle value : " First upgrade complete " - path : mMessage value : " Welcome, pioneer. Your first Hub upgrade is complete. " - path : mAudioEvent value : AdaWelcome - path : mSubtitles value : - Subtitle : " Welcome, pioneer. Your first Hub upgrade is complete. " SenderClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Interface/UI/Message/Sender/Sender_ADA.Sender_ADA_C TimeStamp : 0 - path : mCanBeQueued value : true - path : mCanBeRepeated value : false - path : mBlockedByCooldown value : false - path : mPriority value : 1 - path : mTrigger value : class : /Game/FactoryGame/AvailabilityDependencies/BP_SchematicPurchasedDependency.BP_SchematicPurchasedDependency_C properties : - path : mSchematics value : - /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-1.Schematic_1-1_C - path : mRequireAllSchematicsToBePurchased value : true mAudioEvent is a soft Wwise event reference. The short ID resolves to /KDataForge/GenAssets/ADAExample.Gen_ADAExample_AdaWelcome ; the full path is equivalent. The sound loads before the message’s properties apply. The inline trigger uses the concrete availability-dependency Blueprint; the native base class is abstract. KDataForge registers generated FGMessage instances with the game’s Primary Asset Manager, as required by Satisfactory 1.2. Install the pack before loading the world. When adding a new message to a running world, restart the session so the story subsystem discovers its trigger. The example includes one ADA popup subtitle at the beginning of the recording. For longer audio, add entries to mSubtitles using Subtitle , SenderClass and TimeStamp , with timestamps in seconds matching your recording. If your game version changes the sender asset, choose its current class from the reflection catalog. The Satisfactory ADA guide explains sender and subtitle configuration.

sections.heading: Author and check in the editors
sections.text: Open the pack in the VS Code extension. Use Wwise sound wizard, or create a sound document and add AdaWelcome / audio/welcome.wav in the Sounds form. Optional UI metadata controls its label, help text and section under Options → Audio . Add the recording to audio/ , then create the dataasset document above. Run validation. Unsupported encodings and out-of-pack paths appear in Problems. Go to definition on the AdaWelcome reference should open the sound declaration. Install the complete pack, load a save, and inspect /kdf report . Run /kdf sound ADAExample AdaWelcome to hear the recording through Wwise. If this works but ADA does not speak, inspect the message’s trigger, conditions and queue state separately. Purchase Hub Upgrade 1 to check the message trigger. The in-game editor can inspect the generated message and edit its reflected properties; pack workspace also supports sound entries. After editing the recording or YAML, run /kdf reload on the host. Multiplayer clients need the same pack and recording and must reload locally or restart the session. Changes to an already played, non-repeatable message do not reset its narrative save state.

pages.title: Balancing
pages.description: Editing examples for base-game balance, recipes, items, resources, equipment, consumables, schematics, research, categories, belts, and bulk edits by tag, producer building, ingredient, product, name pattern, or property value.

sections.heading: Balancing
sections.text: Everything below works through type: cdo documents. Every reflected property of every FactoryGame class is addressable this way. Creating new content has its own page per type: Item , Recipe , Schematic , and friends. Start at End-to-End Pack for the tied-together version. Building and machine tuning lives in Power & Machines . ℹ️ Verify property names and asset paths against your game version. The examples on this page use real FactoryGame properties and content paths, but game updates occasionally rename or move them. If a target: path or path: doesn’t resolve, nothing breaks, the load report tells you exactly which patch failed ( /kdf report , see Getting Started → Troubleshooting ). Confirm the effect in-game after every patch.

sections.heading: Recipes ( UFGRecipe )
sections.text: Every craftable recipe in the game, whether base, alternate, or buildable, is backed by a UFGRecipe class default object. This means rebalancing crafting time, ingredient ratios, or output without replacing the recipe outright is just a cdo patch against that class. The properties worth knowing are mDisplayName , mDisplayNameOverride , mIngredients , mProduct , mManufactoringDuration , mManualManufacturingMultiplier , mProducedIn , mRelevantEvents , mVariablePowerConsumptionConstant , mVariablePowerConsumptionFactor , and mGameplayTags . The patch below halves iron ingot smelting time, doubles the ore cost, adds a bonus iron plate to the output, and unlocks the recipe in the Manufacturer as well as the Smelter: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.5 - path : mIngredients[0].Amount value : 2 - path : mProduct op : append value : ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlate/Desc_IronPlate.Desc_IronPlate_C Amount : 1 - path : mProducedIn op : append value : /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/ManufacturerMk1/Build_ManufacturerMk1.Build_ManufacturerMk1_C

sections.heading: Items ( UFGItemDescriptor )
sections.text: UFGItemDescriptor is the base class behind every stackable item in the game. It drives how the item stacks, what it burns for, how much radiation it emits, where it sorts in the build menu, and its display text. Balancing an item’s inventory footprint or fuel value means patching one of mDisplayName , mDescription , mAbbreviatedDisplayName , mStackSize , mForm , mEnergyValue , mRadioactiveDecay , mCanBeDiscarded , mRememberPickUp , mResourceSinkPoints , mSmallIcon , mPersistentBigIcon , mCategory , mSubCategories , mMenuPriority , mFluidColor , mGasColor , mIsAlienItem , or mGameplayTags . The example below bumps iron ingots to the largest stack bucket, rewrites its tooltip description, and doubles the AWESOME Sink points earned for scrapping it: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mStackSize value : SS_HUGE # EStackSize enum: SS_ONE/SS_SMALL/SS_MEDIUM/SS_BIG/SS_HUGE/SS_FLUID - path : mDescription value : key : IronIngot_Desc ns : MyPack source : Now stacks higher. - path : mResourceSinkPoints op : multiply value : 2 ⚠️ mStackSize is an enum, not a count. EStackSize has exactly six buckets ( SS_ONE … SS_HUGE , plus SS_FLUID ). It isn’t “items per stack” as a number, so always set it by name. It’s also cached by the engine : writing it on the CDO alone would change nothing in-game (KBFL ships a dedicated UKBFLCDOItemStackSize helper for exactly this reason). KDataForge handles the cache automatically. Any op that writes mStackSize on an FGItemDescriptor -derived target also resets the descriptor’s cached stack size ( mCachedStackSize ), so the example above works out of the box. Two things to know: inventories that already contain the item may need the item re-added (or a game reload) before existing slots reflect the new limit. Also, if you use KBFL’s own CDO assets for stack sizes, don’t patch the same descriptor from both sides. See YAML Schema → Special-cased properties .

sections.heading: Resources ( UFGResourceDescriptor ) & fluids/gases
sections.text: Raw resources, fluids, and gases extend the same UFGItemDescriptor chain but add a handful of fields that only make sense for non-solid items: mForm selects solid/liquid/gas, and mFluidColor / mGasColor drive the color used for pipe contents, tank fill levels, and the resource icon in the UI. Recoloring a fluid or changing its form uses those fields directly: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/Water/Desc_Water.Desc_Water_C properties : - path : mFluidColor value : R : 20 G : 120 B : 255 A : 255 - path : mForm value : RF_LIQUID

sections.heading: Equipment & consumables ( UFGEquipmentDescriptor , UFGConsumableDescriptor )
sections.text: Descriptor subclasses inherit every UFGItemDescriptor property. Equipment adds, for example, mEquipmentClass (soft class), while consumables add health and consume properties. type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Equipment/Chainsaw/Desc_Chainsaw.Desc_Chainsaw_C properties : - path : mEnergyValue value : 0

sections.heading: Removing radioactivity
sections.text: mRadioactiveDecay on the item descriptor drives the radiation emitted by held or stored items. set it to 0 on the nuclear items: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/OreUranium/Desc_OreUranium.Desc_OreUranium_C properties : - path : mRadioactiveDecay value : 0 - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/NuclearWaste/Desc_NuclearWaste.Desc_NuclearWaste_C properties : - path : mRadioactiveDecay value : 0 Repeat the patch entry for every radioactive descriptor you want to neutralise (uranium fuel rods, plutonium parts, …).

sections.heading: Conveyor belt speed: ALL belts at once
sections.text: Every belt mark derives from the native AFGBuildableConveyorBelt , so one subclass-expanded patch covers Mk.1 through Mk.6 (and modded belts!): type : cdo patches : - target : /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableConveyorBelt applyToSubclasses : true # Mk.1–Mk.6 + every modded belt class properties : - path : mSpeed op : multiply value : 2 ℹ️ mSpeed is not items/min. It is stored in the engine’s internal unit (cm/s scaled by 2), so a Mk.1 belt’s “60 items/min” is not 60 here. Prefer relative ops ( multiply ) over absolute set values, and verify the resulting throughput in-game.

sections.heading: Schematics ( UFGSchematic )
sections.text: UFGSchematic backs every unlockable in the game: HUB milestones, MAM research nodes, and AWESOME Shop entries alike. It’s the single class to patch whether you’re rebalancing progression cost, research time, or which tier something unlocks at. The properties in play are mType , mDisplayName , mDescription , mSchematicCategory , mSubCategories , mMenuPriority , mTechTier , mCost , mTimeToComplete , mUnlocks , mSchematicIcon , mSmallSchematicIcon , mSchematicDependencies , mHiddenUntilDependenciesMet , and mRelevantEvents . The patch below shrinks a tutorial schematic’s completion time to a tenth, clears its cost array so it’s free, and clamps its tech tier into the valid range from 0 to 9 : type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Tutorial/Schematic_Tutorial1.Schematic_Tutorial1_C properties : - path : mTimeToComplete op : multiply value : 0.1 - path : mCost op : clear # free! - path : mTechTier op : clamp min : 0 max : 9

sections.heading: Making a milestone free
sections.text: Same mechanism, applied to a HUB milestone: clear the cost array and set the cooldown to (nearly) nothing: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-1.Schematic_1-1_C properties : - path : mCost op : clear # no item cost - path : mTimeToComplete value : 1 # 1-second freighter turnaround

sections.heading: Research / M.A.M. ( UFGResearchTree )
sections.text: M.A.M. research trees are their own class, UFGResearchTree , separate from the schematic nodes they unlock. This class supplies the tree’s own display name and grouping in the M.A.M. menu. Renaming a tree, for a total-conversion pack or just to fix a typo, is a one-line patch against that display name: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Research/Mycelia_RS/ResearchTree_Mycelia.ResearchTree_Mycelia_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : ' Mycelia (Rebalanced) '

sections.heading: Categories ( UFGItemCategory , UFGSchematicCategory )
sections.text: Categories are the group headers shown above rows of items in the inventory and build menus, and above schematic groups in the M.A.M. and AWESOME Shop. They hold nothing but display metadata, so renaming one is the same mDisplayName patch as any other descriptor. Just target the category asset instead of an item or schematic: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/ItemCategories/Cat_Ingots.Cat_Ingots_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : ' Metals '

sections.heading: Vehicles ( AFGWheeledVehicle )
sections.text: UFGVehicleDescriptor (the buildable-menu entry) only points at the actual vehicle class, the tunable stats live on AFGWheeledVehicle itself, same as any other actor CDO: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Vehicle/Tractor/BP_Tractor.BP_Tractor_C properties : - path : mManualFuelConsumption op : multiply value : 0.75 # 25% less fuel while driven manually - path : mAutopilotFuelConsumption op : multiply value : 0.75 - path : mInventorySize value : 12 applyToSubclasses: true on /Script/FactoryGame.FGWheeledVehicle tunes every vehicle (Tractor, Truck, Explorer, Cyber Wagon, and modded vehicles) in one patch, same as the belt-speed example above.

sections.heading: Trains ( AFGLocomotive )
sections.text: The locomotive’s power draw is an FFloatInterval (idle/full-throttle range), not a flat number: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Vehicle/Train/Locomotive/BP_Locomotive.BP_Locomotive_C properties : - path : mPowerConsumption value : Min : 5 Max : 80 # MW; vanilla is roughly Min 15 and Max 110 There’s no separate top-level “max speed” stat on the locomotive to patch, speed on a given track segment is governed by curvature/signals, not a flat per-locomotive cap.

sections.heading: Creatures ( AFGCreature , AFGCreatureDescriptor )
sections.text: Creature identity/UI lives on the lightweight UFGCreatureDescriptor (mostly just a pointer at the creature class plus arachnophobia-mode icons); combat/movement stats live on AFGCreature itself and its movement data, reflectable the same way. Move speed is a lookup table ( mMoveSpeedData: TArray<FMoveSpeedPair> , one entry per EMoveSpeed , MS_Walk / MS_Run / MS_Sprint ), so target the entry by index rather than a single flat property: type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Character/Creature/Stinger/Char_Stinger.Char_Stinger_C properties : - path : mMoveSpeedData[2].Speed # index 2 = MS_Sprint in the base game's authored order op : multiply value : 0.75 # 25% slower at a sprint ℹ️ Array index isn’t guaranteed by the enum value, confirm which index holds which MoveSpeedType for your target creature (export it from the in-game editor, or check /kdf report after a dry patch) rather than assuming index order matches EMoveSpeed ’s declaration order. ⚠️ Spawner density fields are per-instance, not a class default. AFGCreatureSpawner ( mNumberOfCreatures , mCanSpawnDuringDay / mCanSpawnDuringNight , mRespawnTimeIndays ) controls how many creatures a given spawner produces, but every spawner is a pre-placed level actor , its property values are baked into the map/save data at placement time, the same way an already-built building keeps its saved values after a CDO edit (see Power & Machines → Runtime actor patches ). A cdo patch to AFGCreatureSpawner changes the class default , which only affects spawners that don’t already have their own saved override, in practice, treat this as unverified until you’ve confirmed it in-game on your target save, and prefer patching the creature class itself (as above) for stats that are meant to apply uniformly.

sections.heading: Bulk edits with the tag matcher
sections.text: Patching one target at a time doesn’t scale once you want “every alternate recipe” or “every Tier 3+ schematic” to shift together. matchTag (with a required ofClass scope) finds every CDO or asset of that class, including subclasses, that carries the given gameplay tag, then applies the same ops to all of them in one patch entry. The tag container property is auto-detected, but it can be pinned explicitly with tagProperty when a class exposes more than one. The example below speeds up every recipe carrying the KMods.AlternateRecipe tag by 20%: type : cdo patches : - matchTag : KMods.AlternateRecipe # every recipe carrying this tag … ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe tagProperty : mGameplayTags properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration # … gets 20% faster op : multiply value : 0.8

sections.heading: Buffing all alternate recipes (KAPI tags)
sections.text: KMods.AlternateRecipe is a KAPI-registered native tag, so gate the document behind hasMod . Without KAPI, the tag does not exist and the document is skipped with an Info diagnostic: type : cdo conditions : hasMod : KAPI patches : - matchTag : KMods.AlternateRecipe ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.75 # all alternates 25% faster - path : mVariablePowerConsumptionFactor op : multiply value : 0.9 Registering and matching your own tags works the same way. See Game Tags .

sections.heading: Bulk edits by producer building ( producedIn )
sections.text: Not everything you want to select carries a tag. The most common recipe question is “everything crafted in machine X”, and producedIn: answers it directly. It defaults its scope to FGRecipe , takes one class or a list, and a recipe matches when its mProducedIn references that class or a subclass of it . Full class paths, bare class names, and generated-content ids all work: type : cdo patches : # every Constructor recipe: 25% faster - producedIn : Build_ConstructorMk1_C properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.75 # every Assembler OR Manufacturer recipe: 10% less power (variable-power recipes) - producedIn : - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/AssemblerMk1/Build_AssemblerMk1.Build_AssemblerMk1_C - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/ManufacturerMk1/Build_ManufacturerMk1.Build_ManufacturerMk1_C properties : - path : mVariablePowerConsumptionFactor op : multiply value : 0.9 The subclass rule turns the native base classes into families. Three are worth memorising: producedIn: value Selects every recipe crafted … /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableManufacturer in any manufacturing machine: Constructor, Assembler, Manufacturer, Refinery, Blender, Packager, … and modded machines built on the same base /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildGun with the build gun, that is every buildable’s build recipe /Script/FactoryGame.FGWorkBench by hand at the Craft Bench / Equipment Workshop ( BP_WorkBenchComponent_C and friends derive from it) type : cdo patches : # hand-crafting is twice as fast, everywhere - producedIn : /Script/FactoryGame.FGWorkBench properties : - path : mManualManufacturingMultiplier op : multiply value : 0.5 # every buildable costs 20% less (rounded down by the game per ingredient) - producedIn : /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildGun where : path : mIngredients isEmpty : false properties : - path : mIngredients[0].Amount op : multiply value : 0.8

sections.heading: Bulk edits by ingredient or product
sections.text: ingredient: and product: follow the same rules for mIngredients and mProduct : an item class (or a base class, to catch every item deriving from it), one or many, any-of. They stack with each other and with producedIn: ; every filter on the entry has to hold: type : cdo patches : # everything that consumes Plastic or Rubber crafts 10% faster - ingredient : [ Desc_Plastic_C , Desc_Rubber_C ] properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.9 # every recipe producing Screws in an Assembler yields double - product : Desc_IronScrew_C producedIn : Build_AssemblerMk1_C properties : - path : mProduct[0].Amount op : multiply value : 2 # every recipe that produces ANY equipment (subclass rule on an item base class) - product : /Script/FactoryGame.FGEquipmentDescriptor properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.5 mProduct[0].Amount addresses the first product. Recipes with several outputs need one op per index; a where: clause such as path: mProduct[*].ItemClass / equals: Desc_IronScrew_C does not tell an op which index matched.

sections.heading: Bulk edits by name pattern ( matchName )
sections.text: Vanilla content follows naming conventions, and matchName: lets you select on them without tags. Patterns are case-insensitive wildcards; the _C suffix is optional, and a pattern containing / is matched against the full class path so you can select by content folder: type : cdo patches : # every vanilla alternate recipe, no KAPI dependency needed - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe matchName : Recipe_Alternate_* properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.8 # every milestone (Progression folder) researches twice as fast - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGSchematic matchName : /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/* properties : - path : mTimeToComplete op : multiply value : 0.5

sections.heading: Bulk edits by property value ( where )
sections.text: where: compares any reflected property of every candidate in an ofClass: scope. One map, or a list of maps that must all hold; each map has a path: and exactly one operator ( equals , notEquals , lessThan , lessOrEqual , greaterThan , greaterOrEqual , contains , notContains , matches , isEmpty ). [*] in a path means “any element”: type : cdo patches : # slow recipes (longer than 8 s) that use Iron Ingot get a bit faster - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe where : - path : mManufactoringDuration greaterThan : 8 - path : mIngredients[*].ItemClass equals : Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration op : multiply value : 0.8 # every schematic up to tier 3 unlocks instantly - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGSchematic where : path : mTechTier lessOrEqual : 3 properties : - path : mTimeToComplete value : 0 # every liquid or gas: no sink points (`in` = any of the listed values; enums compare by name) - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGItemDescriptor where : path : mForm in : [ RF_LIQUID , RF_GAS ] properties : - path : mResourceSinkPoints value : 0 # items whose display name mentions "Nuclear" cannot be discarded - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGItemDescriptor where : path : mDisplayName matches : " *Nuclear* " properties : - path : mCanBeDiscarded value : false # recipes with no producer at all become hand-craftable - ofClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe where : path : mProducedIn isEmpty : true properties : - path : mProducedIn op : append value : /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/-Shared/WorkBench/BP_WorkBenchComponent.BP_WorkBenchComponent_C Reference-typed comparisons ( equals / contains / in on a class or soft-class property) match the class or any subclass , the same way producedIn: does, so path: mProducedIn / contains: /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableManufacturer is the long-hand spelling of producedIn: , and path: mProducedIn / in: [Build_ConstructorMk1_C, Build_AssemblerMk1_C] of a two-entry producedIn: list. The full operator table lives on Targeting .

sections.heading: Removing content in bulk
sections.text: The same filters drive remove: . Taking every Particle Accelerator recipe and every tier-8 milestone out of the game is two short documents; the mechanics, save impact, and the recipe-plus-schematic pairing are on Removing Content : type : recipe remove : - producedIn : Build_HadronCollider_C type : schematic remove : - where : path : mTechTier greaterOrEqual : 8

pages.title: A Complete Building
pages.description: The full reference chain for a dynamically created building (buildable class, building descriptor, build recipe, production recipes, schematic, and sinkpoints), in dependency order, in one pack.

sections.heading: A Complete Building
sections.text: This page walks the full reference chain for dynamically created content, in dependency order, with copy-pasteable YAML. Everything lives in one pack: pack.yml ref : MyFactory name : My Factory Pack version : 1.0.0 Every step references the previous one by generated class path . The id: of each entry is the contract that makes those paths deterministic, in the form /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_<Id> (see YAML Schema → generated class identity ). Honest scope callout, read this first A truly new machine with its own mesh or its own logic is out of scope . KDataForge is 2D-only (no mesh import, ever) and generated classes copy their parent’s layout (no new components or reflected properties). This chain re-skins and re-parametrises existing buildable behaviour : your machine looks like and ticks like its parent, but is a separate class with its own build-menu entry, recipes, stats, and save identity. For genuinely new behaviour you need real C++/Blueprint content.

sections.heading: The ordering guarantee
sections.text: You never need include: between these files. Stages run in a fixed order. The whole Items stage, which generates buildables via class , descriptors via building , and items via item , finishes before Recipes starts. Recipes in turn finishes before Schematics starts. Within Items, the generation types are priority-ordered. So every file below can reference every class generated in an earlier step by its /KDataForge/Gen/... path, regardless of file names or scan order.

sections.heading: Step 1: the buildable actor ( type: class )
sections.text: Does type: building create the building actor ? No, type: building generates the descriptor , which is the build-menu entry. The buildable actor , the Build_X_C class placed in the world, generally comes from an existing buildable parent. You define a type: class entry with parent: set to an existing /Game/....Build_*_C , effectively reparenting an existing buildable . There are no custom meshes, since the policy is 2D-only, and no new components. You get the parent’s mesh, connections, and production logic, with your own CDO overrides. 1-buildable.class.yml type : class classes : - id : Build_MyMachine parent : /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/SmelterMk1/Build_SmelterMk1.Build_SmelterMk1_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : Build_MyMachine_Name ns : MyFactory source : Compact Smelter - path : mPowerConsumption value : 12.0 This generates /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Build_MyMachine , a real AFGBuildableManufacturer subclass via the smelter parent.

sections.heading: Step 2: the building descriptor ( type: building )
sections.text: The FGBuildingDescriptor subclass whose mBuildableClass points at the buildable from step 1: 2-descriptor.building.yml type : building buildings : - id : Desc_MyMachine properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : Desc_MyMachine_Name ns : MyFactory source : Compact Smelter - path : mBuildableClass value : /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Build_MyMachine See Buildings for the descriptor-vs-buildable split in general.

sections.heading: Step 3: the build recipe ( type: recipe )
sections.text: Construction recipes are ordinary FGRecipe s whose product is the building descriptor . Their mProducedIn includes the build gun , which is how the game knows a recipe belongs in the build menu: 3-build-recipe.recipe.yml type : recipe recipes : - id : Recipe_Build_MyMachine properties : - path : mDisplayName value : Compact Smelter - path : mIngredients value : - ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlateReinforced/Desc_IronPlateReinforced.Desc_IronPlateReinforced_C Amount : 4 - ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/Rotor/Desc_Rotor.Desc_Rotor_C Amount : 2 - path : mProduct value : - ItemClass : /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Desc_MyMachine Amount : 1 - path : mProducedIn value : - /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildGun

sections.heading: Step 4: production recipes for the machine ( type: recipe )
sections.text: This step defines what the machine can produce: recipes whose mProducedIn is the generated buildable class from step 1. Adding a new item for it to produce shows the item side of the chain too: 4a-output-item.item.yml type : item items : - id : Desc_CompactIngot parent : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : Desc_CompactIngot_Name ns : MyFactory source : Compact Ingot - path : mStackSize value : SS_HUGE Stack-size caveat The engine caches item stack sizes. KDataForge automatically resets the descriptor’s cached stack size ( mCachedStackSize ) whenever an op writes mStackSize , so the value above just works. Inventories that already contain the item may need the item re-added (or a game reload) to reflect a changed limit. Details: YAML Schema → Special-cased properties . 4b-production-recipe.recipe.yml type : recipe recipes : - id : Recipe_CompactIngot properties : - path : mDisplayName value : Compact Ingot - path : mIngredients value : - ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/OreIron/Desc_OreIron.Desc_OreIron_C Amount : 2 - path : mProduct value : - ItemClass : /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Desc_CompactIngot Amount : 1 - path : mManufactoringDuration value : 3.0 - path : mProducedIn value : - /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Build_MyMachine # the step-1 buildable

sections.heading: Step 5: the schematic ( type: schematic )
sections.text: Unlocks both recipes via an instanced FGUnlockRecipe : 5-schematic.schematic.yml type : schematic schematics : - id : Schematic_MyMachine properties : - path : mDisplayName value : Compact Smelting - path : mType value : EST_Milestone - path : mTechTier value : 2 - path : mCost value : - ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlate/Desc_IronPlate.Desc_IronPlate_C Amount : 100 unlocks : - class : /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties : - path : mRecipes value : - /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Recipe_Build_MyMachine - /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Recipe_CompactIngot Registering the schematic auto-propagates: its recipes register, and the recipes’ items register in turn. The schematic is therefore the only piece you strictly need register: for (see Recipes → auto-propagation ).

sections.heading: Step 6: sinkpoints for the new items ( type: sinkpoints )
sections.text: New items have no AWESOME Sink value until you give them one: 6-sinkpoints.sinkpoints.yml type : sinkpoints track : Default entries : - item : /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Desc_CompactIngot points : 8

sections.heading: Recap: the chain at a glance
sections.text: Six files, six generation steps, each one consuming the class path the previous one produced. The table below is a quick lookup for which file generates what and what it points back at, once you have read the walkthrough above: # File Generates References 1 1-buildable.class.yml buildable actor class existing Build_SmelterMk1_C parent 2 2-descriptor.building.yml building descriptor step 1 via mBuildableClass 3 3-build-recipe.recipe.yml build recipe step 2 as mProduct , FGBuildGun in mProducedIn 4 4a / 4b output item + production recipe step 1 in mProducedIn , item in mProduct 5 5-schematic.schematic.yml schematic steps 3+4 via FGUnlockRecipe 6: Session restart Did you restart after editing YAML? KDataForge reads every document type once during session initialization Ids are the contract. You can rename any file freely, but renaming an id needs a redirects: entry in pack.yml (see Conditions & Packs ). Custom Classes explains the generic generation escape hatch used in step 1. The Buildings , Recipes , Schematics , and Sink Points pages cover each later capability. Use the content-creation schema for exact fields. End-to-End Pack is the item-centric counterpart to this building walkthrough.

pages.title: Delivery Task Trees
pages.description: A complete UKAPIDeliveryTask tree with every property set on every node five nodes including negative coordinates, multi-flag mParentTask, the full Endless field set, how completing a task unlocks more of the tree, and a schematic force-unlock example.

sections.heading: Delivery Task Trees
sections.text: UKAPIDeliveryTask is KAPI's 2D research-tree node type: a small reward/task, placed on an integer coordinate grid, that unlocks once its neighboring parent node(s) are completed. This feature has no Satisfactory Plus dependency it only needs KAPI + KPrivateCodeLib, so it's usable from any mod that links those two. This page builds one complete tree end to end. For every other KAPI data asset type, see Adding KAPI Data Assets; for the underlying YAML grammar mParentTask uses, see Value Forms.

sections.heading: The grid and `mParentTask`
sections.text: Each node has an mCoordinate (FIntVector2 with X and Y fields; negative values are perfectly valid, the grid isn't anchored to the origin) and an mParentTask bitmask using EKAPIDeliveryTaskParent. Each flag maps to a bit and fixed coordinate offset **relative to the node itself**: | Flag | Mask | Parent is at | | None | 0 | no parent | | Above | 1 | (X, Y - 1) | | Left | 2 | (X - 1, Y) | | Right | 4 | (X + 1, Y) | | Bottom | 8 | (X, Y + 1) | | AboveLeft | 16 | (X - 1, Y - 1) | | AboveRight | 32 | (X + 1, Y - 1) | | BelowLeft | 64 | (X - 1, Y + 1) | | BelowRight | 128 | (X + 1, Y + 1) | Every flag set on a node must point at a coordinate some other node in the tree actually occupies, or the node is rejected at load time. Use one flag name for one parent and a YAML sequence for multiple parents. When property metadata and the loaded enum are available under WITH_METADATA, KDataForge resolves and ORs scalar names, sequences, and |-joined strings ("Above|Left"). EKAPIDeliveryTaskParent declares mask values, so Above (1) and Left (2) combine to 3. Raw integer masks such as 3 are accepted by set only; append/prepend and remove require names. If property metadata is stripped or the enum cannot be resolved, this integer property uses ordinary numeric conversion; named bitmask forms and mutations are unavailable. Shipping builds must retain metadata for these named examples. See Property Types for mask-value versus bit-index rules and width limits. mRequiredParentCompletions defaults to 1 and raises the completed-run threshold for every marked parent. This is useful behind an endless parent: - path: mParentTask value: Bottom - path: mRequiredParentCompletions value: 10 Values below 1 are rejected. A queued parent can satisfy default one-run topology so its child can be placed later in same queue. Thresholds above 1 count completed runs only; queued repeats do not unlock or pre-queue child.

sections.heading: Supporting assets
sections.text: The tree below sets every applicable property on every node, including the icon, ADA message, and Endless-only amount-multiplier curve those fields reference. Those three are generated by a small support file, include:-ed so they load first (dataasset/curve/asset all run in the same Assets stage, so ordering across document types is otherwise just file order, not implicit see Document Structure): # file: showcase-delivery-task-support.yml type: asset assets: - id: DeliveryTaskIcon file: mod-logo.png # pack-relative path any 2D image works as a placeholder --- type: dataasset conditions: hasMod: KAPI assets: - id: AdaMessage_TaskComplete class: /Script/FactoryGame.FGMessage # UFGMessage is a UPrimaryDataAsset, so `dataasset` builds it directly properties: - path: mTitle value: "Delivery Complete" - path: mMessage value: "Another delivery task in the showcase tree has been completed." --- type: curve curveType: float curves: - id: DeliveryTaskAmountMultiplier defaultValue: 1 preInfinityExtrap: constant postInfinityExtrap: linear isEventCurve: false keys: - time: 0 value: 1 interpMode: linear - time: 5 value: 2.5 interpMode: linear

sections.heading: A complete five-node tree
sections.text: This tree deliberately starts off-origin, in negative coordinate space, to show the grid isn't restricted to (0, 0)-anchored positive layouts. Every node sets every UKAPIDataAssetBase common field (mName/mDescription/mIcon/mIsDisabled/mPriority/mTags) and every UKAPIDeliveryTask field common to both variants (mAdaMessages/mToastIcon/mToastText). DeliveryTask_Right is switched to bIsEndless: true to demonstrate the complete Endless-only field set (mPoolElements/mTaskRewards/mMaxTasks/mAmountMultiplierCurve/ mAbsolutMaxItemAmount) that a One-Time node never sets; every other node stays One-Time (bIsEndless: false) and sets the complete One-Time field set (mRewards/mCosts, plus mSchematics on the last node): # file: showcase-delivery-task.dataasset.yml type: dataasset conditions: hasMod: KAPI include: - showcase-delivery-task-support.yml assets: - id: DeliveryTask_Root class: /Script/KAPI.KAPIDeliveryTask properties: # --- UKAPIDataAssetBase common fields --- - path: mName value: "Root Task" - path: mDescription value: "The starting node of the showcase tree.
