Each object is evaluated and optionally inverted before aggregation. Invalid behavior values or malformed condition objects fail closed even if another OR branch matches. An empty array passes under AND and fails under OR. The config: condition accepts one expression string or a nonempty list of expression strings; every expression in the list must be true. At runtime, config: [] is an error and skips the affected pack, document, or list element. Neither ifNotMatch: true nor another matching OR branch hides this error. This requirement does not change the empty outer conditions: [] behavior above. Version ranges use SML's semver syntax: >=1.2.3, ^3.12.0, ~1.2.0, exact 1.2.3, unions with ||.

sections.heading: Dependency Ordering (`include:`)
sections.text: include: lists relative file paths (same pack) whose documents must apply before this one within the same stage. It is ordering, not textual inclusion. Cycles fall back to path order with a warning.

sections.heading: Determinism
sections.text: Apply order is deterministic: dependency-aware pack topology (priority descending and ref ascending among ready packs) → stage → handler (priority descending, root type ascending) → same-stage include: constraints → relative path. KDataForge does not negotiate a multiplayer pack checksum or stream general operations between peers. See Architecture.

pages.title: Task Guides
pages.description: Goal-oriented procedures for building, integrating, debugging, and shipping KDataForge packs.

sections.heading: Task Guides
sections.text: Each page here starts from a goal and walks through however many files and document types it takes to get there. Every page includes complete, working YAML that you can copy directly. Features explains individual capabilities, while Reference provides normative fields and APIs. If this is your first pack, start with Getting Started before the guides below. It builds the smallest possible pack and confirms it loads, then covers /kdf commands, debug logging, the load report, session restarts, and current multiplayer limits. That is the groundwork these guides assume. Page Goal Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock The most common first pack: a new item with a placeholder icon, a recipe that produces it, and a Tier-1 schematic that actually makes it obtainable in a fresh game Custom Research Trees Generate a tree, place MAM schematics into its visual node graph, then extend or prune branches safely Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic Unlocking something new from a schematic you didn’t generate, vanilla, another mod’s, or your own from an earlier pack version Localizing Your Pack Shipping new text in multiple languages and overriding existing vanilla or modded strings without retyping them Tag-Based Bulk Balancing Registering your own gameplay tag and bulk-editing everything carrying it in one patch instead of one patch per target Conditional Multi-Mod Integration Packs Adding bonus content only when another mod (or a specific version or class of it) is present, without a hard dependency Debugging a Pack That Won’t Apply An ordered, top-to-bottom checklist for “my YAML file doesn’t seem to be doing anything” Renaming Content Safely What you can rename in a pack for free, what needs a redirects entry, and the one rename redirects genuinely can’t fix Editing Another Mod’s Data Assets Rebalancing existing KAPI or RefinedR&D PrimaryDataAsset instances without creating a new one and without a hard dependency on the mod that owns them From Live Editor Edits to a Shareable Pack Turning values you tweaked live in /kdf editor into a real YAML pack that survives a restart and that you can hand to other people Player-Configurable Balancing Turning fixed numbers into typed settings players can change (slider, checkbox, dropdown, tag list, text), reading them in patches, templates and conditions, and seeing hot and cold values in play If you’re not sure whether you want a tutorial or a reference page, here is the difference. Task Guides assume you know the basics from Getting Started and are trying to get one specific thing working. Use Features for conceptual and per-capability explanations. Use Examples when you want complete, copy-pasteable packs that wire several capabilities together.

pages.title: Conditional Multi-Mod Integration Packs
pages.description: Adding bonus content only when another mod (or a specific version of it, or just one of its classes) is present, without a hard dependency and without breaking the load for players who don't have it.

sections.heading: Conditional Multi-Mod Integration Packs
sections.text: The goal is for your pack to add extra content when another specific mod is installed: a KAPI data asset, a patch to another mod’s buildable, or a bonus recipe. It must not error, warn, or crash for the majority of players who don’t have that mod. Conditions & Packs already documents every condition key’s syntax individually. This tutorial covers the missing piece: how the pieces actually behave under the hood, and how to combine them into a real optional-integration pack.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.text: conditions: is a top-level key accepted by every document type, including cdo , item , dataasset , schematic , and more. It accepts one condition object or an array of condition objects. Keys in an object are AND-combined . An object’s optional ifNotMatch: true field negates that object’s combined result. Top-level conditionBehaivor: AND|OR combines array objects and defaults to AND . type : cdo conditions : hasMod : KAPI patches : - target : /Script/KAPI.KAPIDataAssetBase # ... If the combined condition result fails, KDFConditionEvaluator::Evaluate returns false for that document. The document is dropped before its handler ever runs, so no properties: , no patches: , nothing inside it is touched. The loader records a single Info -severity diagnostic ( Skipped by conditions: <reason> ) and moves on to the next document. Nothing else in the pack, or in any other pack, is affected. This is the entire mechanism behind optional integration: write the bonus content as if the other mod is always there, then gate the whole document on a condition that’s false when it isn’t.

sections.heading: hasMod: scalar, sequence, and version-pinned forms
sections.text: conditions : hasMod : KAPI # scalar one mod, any version --- conditions : hasMod : - KAPI - RefinedPower # sequence ALL must be loaded --- conditions : hasMod : RefinedPower@>=4.0.0 # inline version pin, one mod reference --- conditions : hasMod : - KAPI - " RefinedPower@>=4.0.0 " # mix plain refs and pinned refs in one sequence Straight from the evaluator: a scalar value becomes a one-element list, and a sequence becomes a list of strings. Each entry is checked independently : for a sequence, every entry must pass or the whole condition, and therefore the whole document, fails. For each entry, everything before the first @ is the mod reference, trimmed of surrounding whitespace. Everything after @ , if present, is parsed as an SML semver range ( >=1.2.3 , ^1.2.0 , ~1.2.0 , exact 1.2.3 , || unions, see Conditions & Packs ) and checked against that mod’s actual loaded version. No @ means the mod just needs to be loaded, any version. hasMod calls UModLoadingLibrary::GetLoadedModInfo(ModReference, …) . The reference has to match the mod’s actual plugin reference or id exactly, case-sensitive, not a display name.

sections.heading: Requiring mods while excluding another mod or version
sections.text: Use a condition array to separate positive requirements from negated requirements: conditions : - hasMod : - KAPI - KLib - hasMod : IncompatibleMod ifNotMatch : true This applies only when KAPI and KLib are both loaded and IncompatibleMod is absent. The two objects are AND-combined by default. ifNotMatch defaults to false and negates only the object where it is written. Add an inline range to exclude only matching versions: conditions : - hasMod : - KAPI - KLib - hasMod : ' OptionalIntegration@^2.0.0 ' ifNotMatch : true The inverted object passes when OptionalIntegration is absent or when its loaded version does not match ^2.0.0 . It fails only when a matching 2.x version is loaded. The explicit map form works too: conditions : - modVersion : OptionalIntegration : ' ^2.0.0 ' ifNotMatch : true ifNotMatch negates the entire object’s AND result. For example, this passes unless both mods are loaded: conditions : - hasMod : - ModA - ModB ifNotMatch : true To require that neither ModA nor ModB is loaded, use two independently inverted objects instead. Unknown keys, malformed value types, invalid ranges, and a non-boolean ifNotMatch remain configuration errors; inversion never turns them into a match.

sections.heading: Choosing AND or OR across condition objects
sections.text: conditionBehaivor sits beside conditions: and accepts AND or OR case-insensitively. It defaults to AND , preserving packs written before this option existed. Correctly spelled conditionBehavior is also accepted as an alias. conditionBehaivor : OR conditions : - hasMod : RefinedPower - hasMod : FicsitFarming This document applies when either mod is loaded. With AND , both would be required. KDataForge evaluates each object’s internal keys, applies its ifNotMatch , then combines final object results. That makes mixed positive/negative alternatives possible: conditionBehaivor : OR conditions : - hasMod : RefinedPower - hasMod : LegacyPowerBridge ifNotMatch : true This applies when RefinedPower is loaded or LegacyPowerBridge is absent. Invalid behavior values, unknown keys, malformed objects, and invalid ranges always fail closed; a matching OR branch cannot hide them. An empty condition array passes under AND and fails under OR .

sections.heading: modVersion: vs hasMod : what’s actually different
sections.text: modVersion: is an explicit map form: conditions : modVersion : SML : ' >=3.12.0 ' KAPI : ' >=2026.0.0 ' Reading the evaluator, modVersion doesn’t do anything structurally different from hasMod . For every Ref: range entry it builds the exact string "Ref@range" and calls the same EvaluateHasMod function hasMod uses. There is no separate “this is a hard dependency, so assume it’s present and only check the version” code path. Presence is checked every time, for both forms. hasMod (with a pin) modVersion Under the hood EvaluateHasMod("Ref@range", …) Builds "Ref@range" per map entry, calls the same EvaluateHasMod If the mod isn’t loaded at all Document skipped (Info) Identical , document skipped (Info), not a harder failure Idiomatic use One or two optional integrations, inline Several version constraints stated together, typically for mods you already expect to be present Practically, use hasMod (bare or pinned) for content that’s genuinely optional: a mod you have not declared anywhere as a dependency of your own plugin. Reach for modVersion when you want to state, in one readable block, the version floor for several mods you already treat as real dependencies, whether declared in your own .uplugin or bundled together in a modpack. It reads better than several separate hasMod entries, but it will not error louder if one of those mods turns out to be missing. If a mod is truly required for your pack to make sense at all, that’s a job for your .uplugin ’s own Plugins: dependency list. SML refuses to load your mod if a real dependency is missing. conditions: only ever produces a quiet per-document skip, never a hard failure.

sections.heading: hasClass: gating on a class existing, no mod dependency needed
sections.text: conditions : hasClass : /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableFrackingActivator # scalar one class conditions : hasClass : # sequence ALL must exist - /Script/RefinedPower.RPWindTurbine - /Game/FicsitFarming/Buildable/FarmPlot/Build_FarmPlot.Build_FarmPlot_C hasClass resolves each entry with the exact same class-path resolver KDataForge uses for every target: / class: / parent: reference elsewhere ( FKDFValueCodec::ResolveClass ). It accepts a full /Script/Module.Class or /Game/....Asset_C path, with an automatic _C retry for Blueprint classes written without the suffix. As a last resort, for name-only input with no / or . at all, it falls back to a bare-class-name lookup against whatever’s currently loaded in memory. Ambiguous matches log an error and pick the first sorted match, so use full paths in anything you publish. The reason hasClass exists alongside hasMod is what happens when the check fails silently vs. loudly . A cdo document whose target: (or allAssetsOfClass: ) points at a class that doesn’t resolve produces an Error diagnostic: the class was expected to be there and wasn’t. Wrap the same patch in a conditions: block with hasClass: and a missing class instead produces the quiet Info-level “skipped by conditions” message, and nothing else happens. That’s the whole value of hasClass for optional integration: it turns “this class doesn’t exist” from a load error into an expected, silent no-op. It does that without your pack, or its .uplugin if it has one, needing to declare a dependency on the other mod at all, since you’re checking for the class directly rather than asking SML whether a specific plugin id is loaded.

sections.heading: Combining conditions in one block (AND)
sections.text: Every key inside one conditions: map is ANDed together, so you can require several independent things at once: type : schematic conditions : hasMod : KAPI gameVersion : ' >=416000.0.0 ' schematics : - id : Schematic_KAPIBonusResearch properties : - path : mDisplayName value : KAPI Integration Research # ... unlocks a recipe that only makes sense once KAPI's data assets exist This schematic only applies when both KAPI is loaded and the game build is recent enough. If either one is false, the whole document (research entry, unlock, everything) is skipped as a unit, with one Info diagnostic naming whichever condition failed first.

sections.heading: Worked scenario: base content + two independent optional integrations
sections.text: A pack that always ships a base item, then layers on two independent bonuses: one gated by hasMod , one by hasClass . Neither blocks the other, or the base item, if its target mod is missing.

sections.heading: (a) The base item: always applies, no conditions
sections.text: # file: super-ingot.item.yml (excerpt no conditions: key at all) type : item items : - id : SuperIngot parent : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : Super Ingot Every player gets the item, the recipe, and the schematic that unlocks it. See Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock for that full chain. Nothing about it depends on any other mod.

sections.heading: (b) A KAPI data asset: only if KAPI is loaded
sections.text: super-ingot-cleaner.dataasset.yml type : dataasset conditions : hasMod : KAPI assets : - id : CleanerItem_SuperIngot class : /Script/KAPI.KAPICleanerItemDescription properties : - path : mProductionTime value : 6.0 - path : mInFluid value : ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/Water/Desc_Water.Desc_Water_C Amount : 500 This is the standard shape for KAPI-integrated content. See Data Assets for the full field reference. If KAPI isn’t installed, this document is skipped and the base item from (a) is completely unaffected.

sections.heading: (c) A RefinedPower patch: only if the class actually exists
sections.text: refinedpower-windturbine-boost.cdo.yml type : cdo conditions : hasClass : /Script/RefinedPower.RPWindTurbine patches : - target : /Script/RefinedPower.RPWindTurbine applyToSubclasses : true properties : - path : mMaxTurbinePowerProduction op : multiply value : 1.25 This pack never lists RefinedPower as a dependency anywhere. hasClass checks for the actual ARPTurbineBaseActor -derived class at load time and skips cleanly (Info, no error) if it’s absent. This is the same no-hard-dependency philosophy as the RRDA integration pattern already documented in Data Assets → Editing RefinedR&D data assets (RRDA) . That pattern gates on hasMod: RefinedRDApi because it’s patching RRDA’s own data assets, whose consumer rescan already runs by reflection. Here, we go one level more direct and gate on the RefinedPower class itself with hasClass . This is useful whenever you want to touch another mod’s actual buildable/actor class rather than a data asset built for cross-mod integration. Three independent documents, three independent outcomes: (a) always applies, (b) applies only with KAPI, (c) applies only with RefinedPower present. Any subset, “only (a)”, “(a)+(b)”, “(a)+(c)”, or all three, is a valid, error-free load depending on what’s actually installed.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: A document seems to be silently doing nothing, no errors anywhere. This is very likely a failed condition. Today, /kdf report only prints Warning / Error diagnostics and only counts those two severities in its summary line. A condition failure is Info severity and is filtered out of both, so there’s no explicit “Skipped by conditions” line to read in the chat output right now. The indirect tell is the summary’s “N document(s) applied” count: a condition-skipped document never gets counted there. So if that number is lower than the number of .yml files you expect to apply, a condition mismatch on one of them is the most likely cause. Temporarily delete the conditions: block to confirm the rest of the document is otherwise correct, then reintroduce it. A condition that should pass never does. The single most common cause is a typo’d mod reference: hasMod / modVersion match the mod’s exact plugin reference, case-sensitive ( KAPI , not Kapi or kapi ). Double check the spelling against the actual mod’s .uplugin SemVersion /reference id, not its display name in the mod list. hasClass never passes even though the mod is definitely installed. Check for a missing _C on a Blueprint class, or a class that only exists in a newer/older version of that mod than what’s installed. hasClass checks the class as it exists right now, not a version range, so pair it with hasMod: OtherMod@>=X.Y.Z in the same block if you need both. Want the load to hard-fail instead of quietly skipping when a mod is missing? conditions: never does that, by design: diagnostics are never fatal. If a mod is a genuine hard requirement, declare it in your own .uplugin ’s dependency list instead. SML will refuse to load your mod at all rather than silently skip content. Conditions & Packs is the syntax reference for condition keys, pack.yml , redirects: , and include: . Data Assets documents type: dataasset and the RefinedR&D integration pattern used above.

pages.title: Debugging a Pack That Won't Apply
pages.description: An ordered, top-to-bottom checklist for "my YAML file doesn't seem to be doing anything." Six checkpoints, from file discovery to session initialization.

sections.heading: Debugging a Pack That Won't Apply
sections.text: Every other page in Features has its own scattered “Troubleshooting” section for symptoms specific to that document type. This page is different. It’s the one ordered sequence you follow top to bottom the moment something you wrote just isn’t happening and you don’t yet know why. Each step below rules out exactly one stage of the pipeline before you move to the next, so don’t skip ahead. The six steps mirror the real pipeline, in the real order it runs ( Source/KDataForge/Private/Subsystems/KDFSubsystem.cpp ): scan → parse/type-detect → conditions → validate → apply → restart scope when testing YAML changes.

sections.heading: Step 1: is the file even being scanned?
sections.text: KDataForge starts at the Unreal project root, which is FactoryGame/ in a packaged game, and walks up to 6 levels deep . A directory becomes a pack root when it is named DataForge , uses the legacy name data-editor , or directly contains pack.yml . Names are case-insensitive. While walking, the scanner prunes Content , Saved , Intermediate , Binaries , DerivedDataCache , Plugins , Source , and Config , so a root nested inside one of those directories is never found. Everything below a detected root is scanned for *.yml and *.yaml . The one exception is pack.yml , which is read separately as the manifest. Roots may nest; each file belongs to its deepest enclosing root, never both the child and parent pack. Run /kdf report . The first line is always: KDataForge: N pack(s), N document(s) applied, N op(s), N actor patch(es), N error(s), N warning(s) If the pack count didn’t change after adding your folder , it wasn’t found. Check the exact root marker ( DataForge , data-editor , or a direct pack.yml ), its depth from the project root, and that no parent directory in the path matches the pruned list above. A pack directory that resolves but has enabled: false in pack.yml is excluded from the pack count entirely. It’s never added to the pack list, and it produces only an Info-level “Pack ’…’ is disabled, skipped” diagnostic. See Step 3 for why that won’t show up in the report text either. A disabled pack therefore looks identical, from the report’s perspective, to a pack that was never found at all. Two packs resolving to the same ref : the second directory is skipped entirely with a Warning, “Duplicate pack ref ’…’, directory skipped.” This is visible in /kdf report . If your pack doesn’t even move the pack/document counts, nothing past this point matters yet. Fix the location first.

sections.heading: Step 2: did the root type resolve?
sections.text: First confirm the file parsed. Malformed YAML is an Error ; that file is skipped, while every other file continues through the load. Fix the YAML parse failed diagnostic before checking its root type. A document’s type comes from either an explicit type: key or the <name>.<type>.yml filename convention (e.g. super-ingot.item.yml implies type: item ). There are two distinct ways this can go wrong, and they look different in the report. No type could be determined at all happens when there’s no type: key and the filename doesn’t match the convention either. This produces one Warning per offending file , from ScanAndParse : [Warning] my-pack/mystery-item.yml: No 'type:' key and no '<name>.<type>.yml' filename convention document skipped A type was determined, but no handler owns it happens with a typo like type: reciept , a <name>.reciept.yml filename, or a type that belongs to a mod you don’t have loaded. This warns only once per distinct type string across the entire load , not once per file: [Warning] my-pack/typo.reciept.yml: No handler registered for document type 'reciept' (planned for a later phase?) That dedup matters. If you copy-pasted the same typo into five files, you’ll only see one warning line, not five, so don’t assume only the reported file is affected. Both lines follow FKDFDiagnostic::ToString() ’s exact contract: [Severity] file: message , or [Severity] file:line: message when a line number is known. Most scan/type diagnostics don’t carry one, since they’re about the file as a whole, not one YAML node.

sections.heading: Step 3: did conditions pass?
sections.text: A conditions: object or array ( gameVersion , hasMod , modVersion , hasClass , per-object ifNotMatch , and top-level conditionBehaivor: AND|OR , see Conditions & Packs → Conditions ) is evaluated once per document, before validation or apply. A failing condition produces exactly one diagnostic: Skipped by conditions: Required mod 'SomeMod' is not loaded This diagnostic is Info severity, and BuildReportString (the text behind /kdf report ) explicitly skips every Info -severity entry before printing. That’s not a report-formatting quirk you can work around with a flag. The same filtered string is also what the in-game editor’s load report scans for [Error] / [Warning] to decide whether to flag a problem, so a condition typo produces zero visible signal anywhere a player normally looks . The document is silently skipped, every single time, and neither /kdf report nor the in-game editor will ever mention it. There is currently no player-facing switch that surfaces Info diagnostics: no debug-log line, no /kdf report -v , nothing. The condition evaluator itself doesn’t log anything either. It only ever returns a fail reason string that the framework then buries at Info severity. The only reliable way to catch this today is to temporarily delete or comment out the document’s conditions: block and restart the session. If your document suddenly counts toward “document(s) applied” (or your op’s debug line from Step 5 appears) with the block removed, the condition was the culprit. Put the block back and check it against Conditions & Packs for exact key names, mod ref spelling, version-range syntax ( gameVersion / hasMod / modVersion all use SML semver ranges), and array grouping ( ifNotMatch negates only its containing object), and conditionBehaivor spelling/ value ( AND is default; conditionBehavior is accepted as an alias).

sections.heading: Step 4: did the document validate?
sections.text: Every handler runs ValidateDocument before ApplyDocument . The two check fundamentally different things. ValidateDocument is structural. Is the document even shaped correctly? Missing required keys, wrong node kind (map vs. sequence), or malformed op entries would all fail here. This runs purely against the parsed YAML, so it never touches the live game and can’t fail because a class doesn’t exist. Failures here are Error -severity and often carry a real line number ( Entry->Line ), because they’re about one specific YAML node. Example, from type: cdo : [Error] my-pack/bad.cdo.yml:12: 'matchTag', 'matchName' and 'where' require an 'ofClass' scope class (only the recipe shortcuts 'producedIn', 'ingredient', 'product' default to FGRecipe) If ValidateDocument returns false , ApplyDocument is never called for that document. It’s zero ops, and the document doesn’t count toward “document(s) applied” in the report at all. ApplyDocument is semantic. Now it resolves your YAML against the actual running game. Does target: point at a real, loadable class or object? Does matchTag / producedIn / where + ofClass actually match anything? This is where a structurally-perfect document can still fail because a path is wrong or a class doesn’t exist: [Error] my-pack/bad.cdo.yml: Target '/Game/Typo/Path.Path_C' is neither a loadable class nor object (...) Critically, these failures are per patch entry, not per document . One bad target: inside a document with several patch entries only skips that entry. The rest still apply, and the document still counts as applied as long as at least one entry succeeded. So an Error with a line number pointing at your YAML structure means Step 4a: fix the shape. An Error naming an unresolved path/class means Step 4b: fix the reference, or check spelling and the _C suffix (see Targeting → Choosing a selector ).

sections.heading: Step 5: did the specific op apply?
sections.text: If you’ve gotten this far (the file is found, the type resolved, conditions passed, and the document validated and applied with no errors) but the specific value you expected to change still looks vanilla, turn on debug logging: Per document : debug: true at the top level of the file. Per pack : debug: true in pack.yml . Global : console variable KDF.Debug 1 (or launch with -KDFDebug ), or /kdf debug on from chat. This also logs ops originating from the in-game editor. Every successfully applied op logs exactly one line at Log verbosity from FKDFPatchUtil::LogAppliedOp : [KDF DEBUG] <file>: <target>.<property> <op> : <pre> -> <post> For example: [KDF DEBUG] faster-smelting.cdo.yml: /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C.mManufactoringDuration multiply : 2.000000 -> 1.000000 There are two outcomes here. Your op’s line never appears at all : it never reached the apply step. That means one of Steps 1 to 4 above is still the real problem. Most often the property path silently resolved to a different object than you expected, or the op failed and produced an Error you missed in /kdf report . A failed op logs nothing here; it only ever logs on success. Your op’s line appears, but the pre/post values aren’t what you assumed : the pipeline worked exactly as written. Your assumption about which property holds the value (or its starting value) was wrong. Compare <pre> against what you expected the vanilla value to be before writing more YAML. The log lives at %LOCALAPPDATA%\FactoryGame\Saved\Logs\FactoryGame.log in a packaged game. Search for [KDF DEBUG] .

sections.heading: Step 6: did you reload or restart the session?
sections.text: Save the file, run /kdf reload as host/server administrator, then inspect /kdf report . Reload restores reflected property baselines before re-applying every current file, so additive operations do not stack. Changes to frozen content registrations and other restart-bound state still require a game or dedicated-server session restart; see Smart reload .

sections.heading: Quick reference
sections.text: Step Question What to check 1: Scanning Did the pack/document count in /kdf report change at all? Root marker ( DataForge , data-editor , or direct pack.yml ), depth ≤ 6 from the project root, not nested inside a pruned directory, file extension .yml / .yaml 2: Type resolution Is there a [Warning] about no type / no handler for the type? type: key spelling, <name>.<type>.yml filename convention, typo in a known type name (remember: the “no handler” warning is deduped to one per type, not one per file) 3: Conditions Does the document have a conditions: block at all? Comment it out and reload. If the document suddenly applies, the condition (not the report) was hiding the skip. /kdf report never shows condition-skips, they’re Info-severity and filtered out 4: Validation/Apply Is there an [Error] in /kdf report , with or without a line number? Line number present means structural ( ValidateDocument ), fix the YAML shape. No line number, naming a path/class, means semantic ( ApplyDocument ), fix the reference 5: Op-level apply Turn on debug: true / KDF.Debug 1 . Does your op’s [KDF DEBUG] line appear? Missing entirely means it never reached apply, back to Steps 1 to 4. Present but wrong pre/post means a property/assumption issue, not a pipeline bug 6: Reload boundary Did you run /kdf reload , and does this feature need a restart? Property patches reload live; frozen registrations and irreversible world changes follow the documented restart boundaries Getting Started → Debugging covers all three debug switches and the log location. Its report severity table defines the Info, Warning, and Error levels used here. Diagnostics, never failures explains why a skipped patch entry never halts the rest of the load.

pages.title: Editing Another Mod's Data Assets
pages.description: Rebalancing existing KAPI or RefinedR&D data asset instances without creating a new one and without a hard dependency on the mod that owns them.

sections.heading: Editing Another Mod's Data Assets
sections.text: You don’t want to add a new miner resource, cleaner recipe, or boiler. You want to retune the ones that already exist , whether they belong to KAPI itself or to a RefinedR&D mod (RefinedPower, FicsitFarming). You also want your pack to skip cleanly instead of erroring if that mod isn’t installed. This is a plain cdo patch with a conditions: gate, and no special document type is involved.

sections.heading: The mental model: it’s the same cdo patch you already know
sections.text: UDataAsset instances are objects sitting in memory just like a recipe or schematic CDO. KAPI and many RefinedR&D assets derive from UPrimaryDataAsset , which matters for consumer discovery, but KDataForge edits both primary and plain data assets with the exact same type: cdo document, the same properties: op grammar, and the same target: / allAssetsOfClass: / matchTag: selectors used everywhere else in this framework. There’s no “data asset patch” document. type: dataasset is a different, narrower tool. It only creates a brand-new instance (package /KDataForge/GenAssets/<PackRef> , announced to the asset registry). Once that instance exists, whether type: dataasset made it or the target mod shipped it, you tune it exactly like this tutorial shows. See Data Assets → Creating new instances if you actually do want to create one from scratch instead. One more contrast is worth keeping in mind. Schematics need register: false when you reach into one you don’t own (see Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic ), because register-only mode still touches SML’s content registry. Plain cdo patches on a data-asset instance never register anything. You’re mutating an object that’s already alive, so there’s no register: flag to think about here at all.

sections.heading: Three ways to target an instance, and which to reach for
sections.text: Data Assets → Editing KAPI data assets and Targeting document all three selectors in full; here’s the practical decision for data-asset instances specifically: Selector Use it when… Trade-off target: object path (no _C ) You know exactly which instance, for example only the Iron miner description Fastest and most precise, but you need the exact path. Get it from /kdf editor (browse the asset) or the asset registry. It can change if the owning mod renames the asset allAssetsOfClass: You want every instance of a type retuned the same way, for example every KAPI cleaner recipe or every RefinedR&D boiler The usual default for rebalancing a whole machine family. No path-hunting needed matchTag: + ofClass: You want a subset , for example only the event-tagged miner descriptions Needs the target assets to actually carry a matching tag. KAPI assets implement IGameplayTagAssetInterface , so mTags matches directly with no tagProperty: override needed For a first pass at rebalancing a whole mod’s assets, allAssetsOfClass: is almost always the right starting point. It’s what the worked scenario below uses for both mods.

sections.heading: Worked scenario: bulk-tune two mods, neither as a hard dependency
sections.text: Say you want two independent tweaks. KAPI’s modular miners should produce fluid a bit faster, and every RefinedR&D boiler (RefinedPower’s, FicsitFarming’s, or anyone else’s built on RefinedRDApi) should cook faster too. Neither mod is a dependency of your pack. A conditions: block with hasMod: gates each document so it’s a clean skip, not a hard error, if that mod isn’t loaded. kapi-miner-fluid-tuning.cdo.yml type : cdo conditions : hasMod : KAPI patches : - allAssetsOfClass : /Script/KAPI.KAPIModularMinerDescription properties : - path : mNormalFluidCountPerSecond op : multiply value : 1.25 refinedrd-boiler-tuning.cdo.yml type : cdo conditions : hasMod : RefinedRDApi patches : - allAssetsOfClass : /Script/RefinedRDApi.RRDABoilerDataAsset properties : - path : mDuration op : multiply value : 0.85 These are two separate documents, not one. conditions: gates the whole document , and these two tweaks depend on two different mods being present, so they can’t share a file.

sections.heading: Automatic consumer rescans
sections.text: KAPI and RefinedRDApi cache asset scans. After KDataForge’s initial document load, it rescans an installed consumer only when data assets changed: KAPI’s StartScanForDataAssets is resolved and called through reflection when KAPI is loaded. RefinedRDApi’s equivalent method is resolved the same way. KDataForge has no link or plugin dependency on either mod. Keep hasMod: on a YAML document so class references are skipped cleanly when their owner is absent.

sections.heading: The key-field crash gotcha
sections.text: A handful of properties on KAPI assets are load-bearing enough that the game intentionally crashes if you null them out. Examples include mResourceClass on miner descriptions, mInFluid.ItemClass on cleaner items, and mWidgetClass on tooltip injectors. This tutorial won’t repeat the full list; see Data Assets → key-field warning before you write a set op against any of these. If your goal is “turn this instance off,” use mIsDisabled: true instead. Every KAPI asset has it, and it’s exactly what it’s for.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: The patch silently does nothing : check the exact spelling of your hasMod: value ( KAPI , RefinedRDApi , case matters) and confirm the target mod is actually loaded via /kdf report . A failed conditions: check shows up there as an Info diagnostic, not an error, so it’s easy to miss if you’re only scanning for red text. allAssetsOfClass: matches zero assets : double-check the exact class path ( /Script/KAPI.KAPIModularMinerDescription , /Script/RefinedRDApi.RRDABoilerDataAsset , etc.). A typo’d module or class name matches nothing rather than erroring. /kdf report lists every asset a selector actually matched, so you can confirm the count before you trust the values it set. Values look patched in the report but the in-game behaviour didn’t change : check whether the property you touched is one KAPI/RRDA only reads once at scan time, versus one read live every tick. If it’s the former, confirm the automatic rescan ran after the initial load. If it still looks stale, the more likely cause is a second document overriding the same property later in load order. This guide builds on the full KAPI and RRDA property reference in Data Assets and the selector details in Targeting . For the equivalent “I do not own this, I am extending it” pattern with schematics, see Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic .

pages.title: Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic
pages.description: Unlocking a new or existing recipe from a schematic you didn't generate (vanilla, another mod's, or your own from an earlier pack), with either a direct cdo append or the schematic class shortcut.

sections.heading: Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic
sections.text: Maybe you already have a schematic. It could be vanilla, from another mod, or one you generated in an earlier version of your own pack. Either way, you just want it to also unlock a recipe. Use a direct cdo append when you want the smallest possible patch, or use type: schematic with class: when you prefer the same unlock syntax used for generated schematics.

sections.heading: Direct fix: type: cdo append to mUnlocks
sections.text: mUnlocks is an instanced UObject array. For append , prepend , insert , or set , KDataForge can construct each new entry from a class: plus nested properties: block before adding it to the array. append-extra-recipe.cdo.yml type : cdo patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-2.Schematic_1-2_C properties : - path : mUnlocks op : append value : class : /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties : - path : mRecipes value : - /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Recipe_MyNewRecipe Use a sequence under value: if you want to append several unlock objects in one operation.

sections.heading: Schematic shortcut: type: schematic with class:
sections.text: unlock-extra-recipe.schematic.yml type : schematic schematics : - class : /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-2.Schematic_1-2_C # the EXISTING schematic register : false # it's already registered by the base game don't re-register it unlocks : - class : /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties : - path : mRecipes value : - /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Recipe_MyNewRecipe class: (instead of id: ) tells KDataForge “don’t generate a class, resolve this existing one”. See Type: recipe → register-only mode for the general id: / class: duality, since schematics work the same way. unlocks: applies even in register-only mode . The schematic content-creation handler runs properties: and unlocks: against whatever CDO it resolved, whether that CDO came from generating a new class or from resolving an existing one. This is the one detail that makes the whole pattern work. register: false matters here. register: true (the default) is right when the schematic is yours and this is the first time anything registers it. For a vanilla schematic, or one another mod already registers, it’s already known to UModContentRegistry . You’re only reaching into its CDO to add an extra unlock, not re-announcing its existence. Set register: false to avoid registering it a second time under your mod’s reference.

sections.heading: Same pattern for one of YOUR OWN existing schematics
sections.text: Nothing changes if the schematic is one you generated in an earlier pack version. Just point class: at its generated path instead of a vanilla one, and leave register: false for the same reason: it’s already registered from whichever document first created and registered it. type : schematic schematics : - class : /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Schematic_SuperIngot register : false unlocks : - class : /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties : - path : mRecipes value : - /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Recipe_PureSuperIngot

sections.heading: Unlocking something other than a recipe
sections.text: The same class: + unlocks: shape works for any concrete FGUnlock subclass, not just FGUnlockRecipe . That includes inventory slots, schematics that unlock other schematics, custom unlock types from other mods, and anything else you’d normally put in a schematic’s unlocks: list at generation time. See Type: schematic → Instanced unlocks for the full list of what an unlock entry can configure.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: “class: could not be resolved” : double check the exact path, including the _C suffix for Blueprint schematics. The bare class-name shortcut also works here (see Targeting → bare class name ) if you only know the short name. The recipe registers but the schematic seems to unlock it twice, or you see a warning about duplicate registration : you likely left register: true (the default) on a schematic that’s already registered elsewhere. Add register: false . This is for adding an unlock to something that already exists. For building a brand new schematic from scratch, see Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock instead. The Type: schematic reference covers mType , unlocks: , and generate-versus-register behavior. Type: recipe uses the same id: and class: duality one stage earlier. For the full new-content chain, see Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock .

pages.title: From Live Editor Edits to a Shareable Pack
pages.description: You tweaked values in /kdf editor to see what feels right. Now turn that into a real YAML pack that survives a restart and that you can hand to other people.

sections.heading: From Live Editor Edits to a Shareable Pack
sections.text: You opened /kdf editor , found a recipe or item, dragged a slider, and typed a new number. It felt right immediately. That said, nothing you just did is saved anywhere yet. This tutorial covers the one step between “it works right now” and “it still works next time I launch the game” (or “my friend can install it too”): exporting .

sections.heading: Apply KDataForge operations directly
sections.text: Every editable property row has an OP menu. It contains only operations accepted by that property’s runtime type, using the same validation as a YAML properties: entry. Numeric fields offer arithmetic and clamp ; arrays offer insertion, removal, ordering, replacement, duplication, and deduplication; strings and containers expose their applicable append/prepend/remove/clear operations. copy and move are available for every property. Choosing an operation opens an argument form containing only fields that operation needs: value accepts a normal KDataForge YAML scalar, sequence, or map; clamp asks for min and max ; indexed array operations ask for index and, for swap , with ; copy and move ask for a from property path on the same object; clear , sort , unique , and reverse need no arguments. Apply changes the live object immediately. Invalid YAML, an unsupported value, or an out-of-range index leaves the property unchanged and reports the op-engine error. Undo and Redo also remove and restore the corresponding export entry; move restores both source and destination. Use the inspector search to filter fields by property name, full path, or reflected type. The Ops side tab shows the ordered operation sequence currently queued for the selected object.

sections.heading: Export Diff vs. Export Full
sections.text: Both buttons sit in the editor’s inspector panel, and both call the same underlying export, ExportObjectToYaml . They differ in a single flag, bDiffOnly , and that flag changes what ends up in the file. Export Diff prefers the ordered operations authored in the editor for the selected object. An add , multiply , append , remove_at , copy , or other operation therefore remains that operation in YAML instead of being flattened into a final set . Direct value editing is recorded as set . If no editor-authored operation exists, Diff falls back to properties with a vanilla snapshot recorded during this session. Either way, untouched properties stay absent and continue tracking vanilla or whatever other patches apply to them. Export Full includes every reflected property on the class that is not deprecated, transient, or editor-only. This is broader than the normal Unreal “editable” surface: fields without EditDefaultsOnly / EditAnywhere can still be exported if they are reflected FProperty members. The file is large: the reflected surface of the class, frozen at its current value. The risk is that any vanilla default you never meant to touch gets written into your pack at today’s value. If the base game changes that default later, your pack silently overrides the update. Use Export Diff almost always. The “diff” here really means “session-changed,” not “changed-vs-file-on-disk”. A property counts as changed the moment any op, whether a live edit or an earlier-loaded YAML patch, first touches it in the current session. That’s because this is when FKDFVanillaCache::RecordSnapshot fires, since the first write wins. Properties you only looked at in the inspector never get a snapshot and never show up in a Diff export. Both buttons write to the same place: <ProjectDir>/DataForge/exported/<ObjectName>.cdo.yml This is a source-hardcoded editor staging path. The editor creates DataForge/exported/ automatically when needed. <ProjectDir> is Unreal’s project directory, which is the FactoryGame/ project directory in a packaged game. <ObjectName> is Selected->GetName() . For the common case of editing a recipe, item, or schematic class (its CDO), that name is the engine’s synthetic default-object name. A patch to Recipe_IngotIron_C ’s CDO therefore exports as Default__Recipe_IngotIron_C.cdo.yml , not Recipe_IngotIron.cdo.yml . You don’t need to rename it: KDataForge doesn’t care what the file is called, only what’s inside it.

sections.heading: Moving the export into a real pack
sections.text: <ProjectDir>/DataForge/exported/ sits under a scanner-recognized DataForge root, so a freshly exported file can be discovered on the next session start. That’s not a reason to leave it there, though. exported/ is a scratch folder the editor writes into every time you click the button, so exports from unrelated sessions and experiments pile up there with no grouping and no ref: . Handing a file to someone else means handing them something self-contained: its own folder, its own pack.yml with a stable ref: (the save-persistence contract), not your personal working directory. Before shipping, create a proper author pack and move the file into it: <your-mod>/DataForge/ pack.yml Default__Recipe_IngotIron_C.cdo.yml <-- moved from <ProjectDir>/DataForge/exported/ pack.yml ref : MyTweaks name : My Tweaks version : 1.0.0 The exported file is already valid type: cdo YAML. For the common case of one specific class and one specific patch, you don’t need to touch it at all. You’d hand-edit it when you want to broaden what it applies to: Swap target: /Game/.../Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C for allAssetsOfClass: /Game/.../Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C if you want the patch to also reach subclasses or every asset resolving to that class, not just the one CDO you had selected. Add applyToSubclasses: true alongside target: for the same broadening effect without switching selector kind. Add applyToSpawnedActors: true if this is a buildable and you also want already-placed instances (not just newly spawned ones) to pick up the change. See Targeting for the full selector/modifier reference, and Patching (type: cdo) for the patch shape.

sections.heading: Managing packs inside the in-game editor
sections.text: Switch the editor from Runtime to Packs to work on files instead of live objects. The left pane groups every discovered YAML file below its owning pack.yml . Nested packs are separate: the deepest pack.yml owns a file. Files with invalid YAML remain selectable and open directly in Raw mode so you can repair them. The New pack action creates exactly: <ProjectDir>/Mods/DataForge/<pack-name>/pack.yml Pack names and document names accept letters, digits, _ , and - . Existing files are never overwritten. Select a pack, choose a document type, enter a file name, and click Create . The type list covers every KDataForge root handler: cdo , gametag , asset , localization , class , item , resource , building , unlock , recipe , schematic , research , dataasset , curve , sinkpoints , resourcenode , and sublevel . Each file has two editing surfaces: Form exposes every YAML map, sequence, scalar, and null node. Select a node to replace its complete YAML fragment, add a map member or sequence item, or remove it. Scalar values can also be edited inline. The guided controls provide context-sensitive field and sequence-entry templates for every KDataForge document type. Class-valued rows use a searchable class picker filtered to the expected base class; it includes loaded native classes and Blueprint classes known to the asset registry. Once a target, class, or parent is selected, property-path rows can be chosen from inherited reflected fields, including nested struct and array paths. Operation choices are filtered against the resolved property type, while enum and boolean values offer valid presets. Selecting a properties or where sequence also offers ready-made entries for fields on the resolved class. Raw YAML edits the exact file text, including comments and formatting. Switching back to Form first validates and parses the text. Invalid YAML stays in Raw mode with an error message. Raw edits keep their exact text until a Form mutation occurs. A Form mutation serializes the parsed document again, so comments, quoting choices, and custom whitespace can be normalized or removed. Use Raw mode when those details matter. Save validates YAML syntax and required document shape, writes a temporary file, then replaces the destination atomically. A failed validation or write leaves the previous file intact. Unsaved changes block file/pack switching and closing until you save or explicitly discard them. Save does not apply semantic changes by itself: use /kdf reload for live-safe updates, or restart for content registrations and other startup-only stages.

sections.heading: The Create panel: drafting new content instead of hand-writing YAML
sections.text: The editor’s CREATE section, below the YAML preview, drafts brand-new content: item, resource, building, recipe, schematic, research, unlock, dataasset, or a generic class , without you typing a document by hand. Pick a kind, type an Id , pick a parent class (or class: for dataasset ), optionally pick a registerAs: target for generic class drafts, and click Create . This writes a starting-point document to: <ProjectDir>/DataForge/created/<Id>.<Kind>.yml Create the DataForge/created/ directory before using the action. This is also a staging directory, not the canonical shipping location. For example, MySuperIngot.item.yml . It’s a skeleton: type: , the plural entries key ( items: / recipes: / schematics: / research: / unlocks: / assets: / classes: ), and one entry with id: and parent: (or class: ). There’s no properties: yet. You still add those by hand, same as in Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock , just starting from a correctly-shaped file instead of a blank one. Create writes a draft file; it does not apply the draft to the running session. Every kind, including dataasset , is loaded from YAML on the next session start. The status message shows the written path and reminds you to restart. created/ is a scratch area, so move the finished draft into a real pack before relying on it long-term.

sections.heading: Worked scenario: retuning a recipe’s craft time
sections.text: Open chat, type /kdf editor . Switch to the Recipes category, search for the recipe you want (e.g. the Super Ingot recipe from the item/recipe/schematic tutorial ), and select it. Browser rows show content icons when available: item/building icons, schematic and research-tree icons, recipe product icons, and direct icon properties such as mSmallIcon or mIcon . In the inspector tree, find mManufactoringDuration and commit a new value, say 2.0 instead of 4.0 . The change applies immediately. Go build one and confirm it’s actually faster. Click Export Diff . Because mManufactoringDuration is the only property you touched on this object this session, the exported file is short: type : cdo patches : - target : /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_Recipe_SuperIngot properties : - path : mManufactoringDuration value : 2.0 Check the status bar. It read Exported to <ProjectDir>/DataForge/exported/Default__Gen_KDFSample_Recipe_SuperIngot.cdo.yml (or similar, matching the generated class’s CDO name). Create <your-mod>/DataForge/pack.yml ( ref: MyTweaks ) if you don’t already have a pack folder, and move the exported file in next to it. Restart the game. The recipe still takes 2 seconds: same value, now coming from a real pack file instead of a session-only edit, applied through the identical type: cdo pipeline as before. If you’d clicked Export Full instead, the file would list every reflected, non-deprecated, non-transient, non-editor-only property of the recipe class: ingredients, product, produced-in, display name, and possibly internal reflected fields too. Each value is frozen at its current value, not just the duration. That’s usually more than you want to ship.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Exported file has an empty properties: list or almost nothing under Diff mode. Diff only includes properties that were actually written this session on that specific object . Browsing or inspecting a value without committing an edit never creates a snapshot, so it never shows up. Double-check you selected the same object you edited, and that you actually committed a value, not just opened the row. I edited something, then undid it, then exported, and the property still shows up. The vanilla snapshot is recorded on first write and never cleared by Undo. Diff mode checks “was this property ever touched this session”, not “does it currently differ from vanilla”. So a touched-then-reverted property can still appear in the export, just with its value back at vanilla. This is harmless, it’s a no-op patch, but worth knowing if the file looks odd. Export/Create button seems to do nothing. Check the status bar text at the bottom of the editor window. Both actions always set it: green for success (with the exact file path), or red for failure ( Nothing selected , Could not write <path> , etc.). It’s easy to miss because it’s small, not because the click didn’t register. Can’t find the exported/created file. It is under the source-hardcoded <ProjectDir>/DataForge/exported/ or <ProjectDir>/DataForge/created/ staging directory. The legacy created/ directory must already exist. The Packs workspace creates its own Mods/DataForge/<pack-name>/ directory. Move legacy staging files into a real pack before shipping. Form mode rejects the file. Switch to Raw YAML and repair the syntax. Form requires pack.yml to contain one map, and every normal YAML document root to be a map. Runtime-specific semantic errors are reported when KDataForge loads or reloads the file. New item/recipe/schematic from Create still isn’t there. Create only writes a draft. Move it into a real pack and restart the session. The SML content registry freezes at world begin play. Export Full includes fields from Non-UPROPERTY / Internal . The current UI label is misleading. Those rows are still reflected FProperty members; they only lack Unreal’s normal edit flag or category metadata. Export Full may include them unless they are deprecated, transient, or editor-only. Getting Started covers pack roots, /kdf report , session restarts, and the same debug format used for editor-originated operations. The separate UE Editor Integration workflow uses the WITH_EDITOR -only KDF.ApplyToAssets command to change Unreal Editor assets; it is not the in-game /kdf editor described here. Every export uses the Patching ( type: cdo ) document shape. To fill a Create-panel draft’s properties: from scratch, follow Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock .

pages.title: Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock
pages.description: The most common first pack, a new item with a placeholder icon, a recipe that produces it, and a Tier-1 schematic that actually makes it obtainable in a fresh game.

sections.heading: Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock
sections.text: If you’ve generated an item and can’t find it anywhere in-game, this tutorial is almost certainly the fix. It walks through the complete, minimum chain : item, icon, recipe, schematic, end to end. Every snippet below is a complete, working example, not a hypothetical fragment.

sections.heading: The mistake this tutorial fixes
sections.text: A generated item and a recipe producing it are not enough on their own. Recipe: documents register the recipe class into SML’s UModContentRegistry , so the game knows the class exists. Registration alone doesn’t put the recipe in front of the player, though. Satisfactory gates every recipe behind an unlock , normally granted by a schematic (a HUB milestone or a MAM node). Without a schematic unlocking your recipe, the class exists and the recipe is “known” to the mod content registry, but the player still never sees it. That’s the whole story behind “I don’t see my created item.”

sections.heading: Step 1: the item
sections.text: super-ingot.item.yml type : item items : - id : SuperIngot parent : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SuperIngot_Name ns : KDFSample source : Super Ingot - path : mDescription value : Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well. - path : mStackSize value : SS_HUGE - path : mResourceSinkPoints value : 42 # Placeholder icon see Step 2, loaded by super-ingot-icon.asset.yml - path : mSmallIcon value : /KDataForge/GenAssets/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngotIcon - path : mPersistentBigIcon value : /KDataForge/GenAssets/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngotIcon mStackSize is an EStackSize enum ( SS_ONE / SS_SMALL / SS_MEDIUM / SS_BIG / SS_HUGE / SS_FLUID ), not a plain item count. See Balancing → Items for the full caveat about the engine’s stack-size cache. KDataForge refreshes that cache automatically, so you don’t need to do anything extra. Just don’t write a raw number here expecting it to mean “N items per stack”.

sections.heading: Step 2: a placeholder icon ( type: asset )
sections.text: You don’t need real art to get an item on-screen and testable. Any PNG/JPG/TGA/BMP works, even your mod’s own logo, as a stand-in until you have real icons: super-ingot-icon.asset.yml type : asset assets : - id : SuperIngotIcon file : mod-logo.png # pack-relative path any 2D image Result: /KDataForge/GenAssets/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngotIcon , referenced directly from the item’s mSmallIcon / mPersistentBigIcon in Step 1. No include: needed. type: asset always runs in the Assets stage, and Assets always runs before Items , regardless of file or pack order. See Data Assets for the full type: asset reference. This is the same 2D-image mechanism, just used for an item icon instead of a KAPI data asset.

sections.heading: Step 3: the recipe
sections.text: super-ingot.recipe.yml type : recipe recipes : - id : Recipe_SuperIngot properties : - path : mDisplayName value : ' Super Ingot ' - path : mIngredients value : - ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C Amount : 2 - path : mProduct value : - ItemClass : /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngot Amount : 1 - path : mManufactoringDuration value : 4.0 - path : mProducedIn value : - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/SmelterMk1/Build_SmelterMk1.Build_SmelterMk1_C No include: needed for the item reference. Items always finishes before Recipes starts. This alone gets you a real, registered recipe class, but it’s still locked .

sections.heading: Step 4: the Tier-1 schematic (the step that was missing)
sections.text: super-ingot.schematic.yml type : schematic schematics : - id : Schematic_SuperIngot properties : - path : mType value : EST_Milestone - path : mDisplayName value : Super Ingot Production - path : mDescription value : Unlocks production of the Super Ingot. - path : mTechTier value : 1 - path : mTimeToComplete value : 10 - path : mCost value : - ItemClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C Amount : 20 unlocks : - class : /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties : - path : mRecipes value : - /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_Recipe_SuperIngot mType: EST_Milestone + mTechTier: 1 is what makes this a Tier 1 HUB milestone : the standard “unlocked early, no MAM required” pattern. No include: needed. Recipes always finishes before Schematics starts. register: true is the default, so this schematic (and, via SML’s auto-propagation, the recipe and item it touches) registers into UModContentRegistry automatically. The schematic is the only piece in this whole chain you need registration for. See Type: recipe → auto-propagation . With this file in place, a fresh save now shows “Super Ingot Production” as a purchasable Tier 1 HUB milestone. Purchasing it unlocks Recipe_SuperIngot for the player to build.

sections.heading: Recap: what each file contributes
sections.text: File type: Contributes super-ingot.item.yml item The item class itself super-ingot-icon.asset.yml asset A 2D texture the item references as its icon super-ingot.recipe.yml recipe A recipe producing the item (registered, but locked) super-ingot.schematic.yml schematic The unlock : this is what makes it obtainable

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Item still not appearing after adding the schematic : run /kdf report and confirm all four documents applied with no errors. A typo’d generated-class path (missing pack ref, wrong id spelling) is the most common cause, and it’s always visible there. Icon shows as a checkerboard/missing texture : check that file: is spelled exactly right and is relative to the pack root (the directory containing pack.yml ), not the mod’s own folder. Recipe exists but isn’t selectable at the smelter : the recipe needs the schematic’s unlock applied. In a fresh save that means actually purchasing “Super Ingot Production” in the HUB. Want to unlock a NEW recipe from a schematic that already exists (vanilla or another mod’s, instead of generating your own): that’s a slightly different shape, covered in Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic . For per-document details, use Type: item , Type: recipe , and Type: schematic . Data Assets documents the full type: asset 2D-image mechanism. End-to-End Pack shows a similar chain with localization and sink points.

pages.title: Localizing Your Pack
pages.description: Shipping new text in multiple languages, overriding existing vanilla or modded strings without retyping them, and iterating with translators live with session restarts, without breaking on the next game update.

sections.heading: Localizing Your Pack
sections.text: Two different jobs hide under type: localization . One is adding brand-new text for content you’re creating. The other is overriding text that already exists: vanilla FactoryGame strings, another mod’s, or your own from an earlier pack version. These two jobs use different YAML shapes, and confusing them is the single most common localization bug. This tutorial walks through both, the one-file-per-culture pattern for shipping several languages at once, and the restart-based workflow that makes translator iteration painless.

sections.heading: The two entry forms
sections.text: Every entry under entries: is either a scalar or a block map with source and text fields, and UKDFLocalizationHandler treats them very differently. The scalar form, Key: "some text" , registers a brand-new (namespace, key) pair. It sets both the source and the displayed text to the same string, and you use it for new text nobody has already registered. The map form, Key: with nested source: and text: fields, overrides an existing (namespace, key) pair instead. Here text: is what displays, while source: must match the target’s current source string, and you use it for retexting something that already exists. Omitting source: in the map form makes the handler reuse text: as the source. That’s just the scalar form written longer, and it only works for new keys. ⚠️ The (namespace, key) an entry targets is exactly namespace: (document-level) plus the entry’s own key under entries: . Nothing is inferred. That pair, plus a hash of source: , is what the engine checks before it will display your text: . Get either wrong and nothing errors: you just get an unused row in the localization table that nothing ever reads.

sections.heading: Step 1: give your item a keyed display name
sections.text: Overriding anything later requires the text to have a real (namespace, key) pair in the first place. A plain string mDisplayName is culture-invariant (see Property Types → FText: plain (culture-invariant) ). Invariant text never goes through the localization system at all, so nothing you write under type: localization can ever touch it. Use the keyed map form instead, exactly like the sample pack’s own Super Ingot: # file: super-ingot.item.yml (excerpt) type : item items : - id : SuperIngot properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SuperIngot_Name ns : KDFSample source : Super Ingot ns: KDFSample + key: SuperIngot_Name is now the address every translation for this item’s name has to target.

sections.heading: Step 2: one file per culture
sections.text: Nothing forces you into a single translation file. The natural, idiomatic pattern is one file per language , all targeting the same namespace: /keys. For example, a German file: super-ingot.localization.yml type : localization namespace : KDFSample culture : de entries : SuperIngot_Name : source : Super Ingot text : Superbarren Adding French is just another file with a different culture: . Nothing about the item, the namespace, or the key changes: super-ingot-fr.localization.yml type : localization namespace : KDFSample culture : fr entries : SuperIngot_Name : source : Super Ingot text : Super Lingot Both files apply independently. culture: gates each one against the currently running language, so shipping a dozen languages is a dozen small files, not one giant one. Nothing stops you from grouping several keys from several items into one per-culture file either, once your pack grows past a single item. The namespace/culture gate is per-document, not per-file.

sections.heading: Step 3: overriding an EXISTING text
sections.text: Overriding your own earlier text is trivial: you already know the exact namespace: /key, because you’re the one who chose them in Step 1. Want to retcon the German name later without touching the item file? Add another entry with the map form, same namespace/key, same source: type : localization namespace : KDFSample culture : de entries : SuperIngot_Name : source : ' Super Ingot ' text : ' Ur-Superbarren ' Overriding vanilla or another mod’s text is the same mechanism. You just don’t get to pick the namespace/key. They belong to whatever FText the target already carries, and you have to go find them: Use /kdf editor (works in a normal running game, not just the UE editor). Browse to the target object (a vanilla schematic, another mod’s item, anything KDataForge can resolve) and use Export . If mDisplayName exports as a map containing key , ns , and source , that map is the real address. Copy it verbatim, keep key / ns / source identical, and only change text: . Or read the source mod’s own localization files directly. Most KMods ship Content/Localization/<Mod>/*.archive / .manifest alongside the plugin, which is a faster way to confirm a key than booting the game. If Export shows a plain string instead of a map , the target is culture-invariant. Stop here: there is no (namespace, key) to attach an override to. The only way to change it is a plain cdo patch on the property itself (see Patching (type: cdo) ), which replaces the text for every language at once, not per-culture. Worked example: a schematic whose author (you, an earlier pack version, or another mod) declared mDisplayName with the keyed form: # somewhere upstream the schematic's own properties: - path : mDisplayName value : key : Schematic_SuperIngot_Name ns : MyPack source : ' Super Ingot Production ' # file: fr.localization.yml translating (or retexting) it without touching the schematic type : localization namespace : MyPack culture : fr entries : Schematic_SuperIngot_Name : source : ' Super Ingot Production ' text : ' Production de Super Lingot ' namespace: MyPack + Schematic_SuperIngot_Name has to match the schematic’s declaration character-for-character, and source: has to match the current source string byte-for-byte. Get either one wrong and this document applies cleanly, with no error, while the schematic keeps showing its untranslated name. Recipes are a special case. FGRecipe::mDisplayName is only shown if the recipe’s own mDisplayNameOverride flag is true . Otherwise the UI shows the first product’s item name instead, and a recipe-name translation you write will never be visible no matter how correct it is. If you want a recipe-specific name (and its translations) to actually appear, set mDisplayNameOverride: true alongside mDisplayName in the recipe’s own properties: . Otherwise, translate the produced item’s name instead.

sections.heading: Translation iteration workflow
sections.text: Edit the .yml translation file. Select the matching game language in the Options menu. Restart the session and inspect /kdf report . culture: is evaluated against the language active during session initialization. A culture: fr document is intentionally skipped while the game runs in English.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: A translation applied but nothing changed in-game. This is almost always a source-hash mismatch: source: must be byte-identical to the text’s current stored source (spacing, punctuation, capitalisation), since it’s a hash comparison, not a fuzzy match. If a game update changed the base string, every override keyed off the old one silently stops matching. Copy the string straight out of an /kdf editor Export, never retype it from memory. My override document loads with no errors but the text is still untranslated. Check the namespace: /key pair against exactly what the target FText was declared with, not a name you invented. This is the difference between “new text” and “override”: new keys can use any namespace/key you like, while overrides have to match the target’s real ones exactly. A whole culture file seems to be ignored. Look for a stray or misspelled culture: (e.g. de_DE instead of de-DE , or a typo like germna ). The log line reads skipped: culture <X> does not match current language <Y> when this happens. Omitting culture: entirely applies to every language, which is usually what you want unless you’re intentionally splitting per locale. Overriding a recipe’s display name does nothing. Check mDisplayNameOverride on that recipe: if it’s false , the UI ignores mDisplayName entirely and shows the first product’s item name. Export shows a plain string, not a map containing key , ns , and source . The target text is culture-invariant, so no localization override will ever reach it. Change it with a cdo patch on the property instead (this affects every language, not one). Trying to cdo -patch a schematic/recipe/item you generated yourself, to convert its mDisplayName to the keyed form. CDOChanges runs before Items / Recipes / Schematics in the fixed stage order, so a cdo patch can’t even resolve a KDataForge-generated class’s path yet. Edit the generating document’s own properties: block directly instead ( item.yml / recipe.yml / schematic.yml ). There’s no need for a separate patch for content you’re already generating. Localization is the full reference for entry forms, culture matching, and source hashes. Property Types compares plain and keyed FText forms. Use Patching ( type: cdo ) for invariant text or properties that type: localization cannot reach. The Super Ingot used here comes from Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock .

pages.title: Player-Configurable Balancing
pages.description: Turn fixed pack numbers into settings players can change. Config fields, typed references, templates, config conditions, hot and cold values, and testing in single player and multiplayer.

sections.heading: Player-Configurable Balancing
sections.text: In this guide you give a pack five settings: how fast iron smelts, whether the output is doubled, which tier a milestone appears in, which tags a recipe carries, and a line of description text. You will see hot values change live and a cold value ask for a restart. The files are the configuration part of the KDFSample sample pack, so you can compare them with that pack. Read Pack Configuration first if you want the full rules behind each step. This page is the walkthrough.

sections.heading: What you will build
sections.text: Field Type Apply Used for balance.ironSpeed float slider 0.25 to 4 hot Divides the Iron Ingot smelting time features.enableBonus boolean hot Switches the doubled output on and off features.tier select ( int32 , 1 to 3) cold HUB tier of the Super Ingot milestone tags.extra list of gameplay tags hot Tags added to the Iron Ingot recipe texts.motto multiline text hot First sentence of the Super Ingot description

sections.heading: Step 1: the pack
sections.text: Create DataForge/pack.yml . description and icon are shown next to the pack in settings screens; the icon is a file in the pack folder. pack.yml ref : KDFSample name : KDataForge Sample Pack version : 1.0.0 description : Exercises pack configuration, templates and config conditions. icon : mod-logo.png

sections.heading: Step 2: the categories
sections.text: A settings screen groups fields by category and orders the groups by priority. Categories are ordinary generated classes whose parent is FGCategory . Create DataForge/sample-config-category.class.yml : sample-config-category.class.yml type : class classes : - id : SampleBalanceCategory parent : /Script/FactoryGame.FGCategory properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SampleBalanceCategory_Name ns : KDFSample source : Sample Balance - path : mMenuPriority value : 10 - id : SampleFeaturesCategory parent : /Script/FactoryGame.FGCategory properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SampleFeaturesCategory_Name ns : KDFSample source : Sample Features - path : mMenuPriority value : 20

sections.heading: Step 3: the config definition
sections.text: Create DataForge/kdf-sample.config.yml . The file name ending in .config.yml is what makes it a definition. category: at the top is the default; balance.ironSpeed overrides it. kdf-sample.config.yml type : config category : SampleFeaturesCategory fields : - id : balance.ironSpeed type : number valueType : float name : key : Config_IronSpeed_Name ns : KDFSample source : Iron smelting speed description : How many times faster the Iron Ingot recipe runs than in the base game. tooltip : title : Iron smelting speed text : 1 keeps the vanilla speed, 2 halves the smelting time, 4 is the maximum. category : SampleBalanceCategory default : 2 min : 0.25 max : 4 step : 0.25 decimals : 2 display : slider apply : hot - id : features.enableBonus type : boolean name : Double iron ingot output description : Doubles the amount of Iron Ingots one smelting cycle produces. default : true apply : hot - id : features.tier type : select valueType : int32 name : Super Ingot milestone tier description : HUB tier in which the Super Ingot Production milestone appears. default : 1 options : - value : 1 label : Tier 1 - value : 2 label : Tier 2 - value : 3 label : Tier 3 apply : cold - id : tags.extra type : text valueType : tag multiple : true tagRoot : KDF.Sample name : Extra recipe tags description : Gameplay tags that are added to the Iron Ingot recipe. default : - KDF.Sample.Test maxCount : 4 apply : hot - id : texts.motto type : text valueType : text multiline : true maxLength : 200 name : Super Ingot motto description : The first sentence of the Super Ingot description. default : Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well. apply : hot Every field has a name , a description and (through the field or the document) a category. Start the game once. KDataForge creates FactoryGame/Configs/Packs/KDFSample.config.yml with the defaults.

sections.heading: Step 4: use a value in a patch
sections.text: Typed references replace a whole, unquoted scalar with the field’s typed value. Create DataForge/iron-ingot-faster.cdo.yml : iron-ingot-faster.cdo.yml type : cdo conditions : gameVersion : ' >=1.0.0 ' patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties : # 1. Typed reference: the number 2.0 by default - path : mManufactoringDuration op : divide value : cfg:balance.ironSpeed # 2. Element condition: this operation exists only while the bonus is on - path : mProduct[0].Amount op : multiply value : 2 conditions : config : ' features.enableBonus ' # 3. A list field becomes a list of tags - path : mGameplayTags op : append value : cfg:tags.extra The three operations use all three ways to read a value: cfg:balance.ironSpeed fills the value: with the number. Because the slider’s minimum is 0.25, the division never hits zero. conditions: { config: ... } on the second operation takes the operation out of the list while features.enableBonus is off. It is an element condition and works on any entry of any list. cfg:tags.extra is a list field, so the reference becomes a list.

sections.heading: Step 5: use a value inside text
sections.text: Templates put values into strings. A string that starts with { has to be quoted. Create DataForge/super-ingot.item.yml : super-ingot.item.yml type : item items : - id : SuperIngot parent : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SuperIngot_Name ns : KDFSample source : Super Ingot - path : mDescription value : ' {cfg:texts.motto} Smelts like {item:/Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C:GetItemName} at {cfg:balance.ironSpeed}x speed. ' - path : mStackSize value : SS_HUGE With the defaults the description reads: Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well.
